(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing).

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Sources indicate that even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

According to recent reports, there is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”.

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

Recent findings suggest that as the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching manufacturer Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the latest book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

In a recent development, “If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”.

In a recent development, both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

In a recent development, robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson notes of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”.

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”.

It has been revealed that one of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”.

In a recent development, another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

According to recent reports, “Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Industry observers note that vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.
  • In a recent development, those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

In a recent development, those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Sources indicate that take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Recent findings suggest that don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively swiftly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

Sources indicate that this is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

It has been revealed that don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

According to recent reports, in a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more vital that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

In a recent development, technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other consumers, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other people and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Recent findings suggest that trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

2027 Winter Gear Guide: The Best Skis, Boots, and Outerwear of the Season

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, A SKI Test at Deer Valley, a boot test on Mount Hood, and 430 days testing ski pants later, this is the ski gear worth the money.
  • Recent findings suggest that A skier’s fall ritual: taking inventory of the gear closet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

According to recent reports, A SKI Test at Deer Valley, a boot test on Mount Hood, and 430 days testing ski pants later, this is the ski gear worth the money. (Photo: Re Wikstrom).

Recent findings suggest that A skier’s fall ritual: taking inventory of the gear closet. What stays, what goes? The jacket survived another season, the boots are fine as long as nobody asks questions, and the goggles might be saved by a upcoming lens. Eventually, something has to be replaced, and everything on the ski shop racks has a marketing pitch. The 2027 Winter Gear Guide is our case for what’s actually worth the money.

Our men’s ski pants testers alone logged 430 ski days last season, which is a lot of time to find out whether a pant seat is truly waterproof. Spread that scrutiny across skis, boots, outerwear, and accessories and you get the 2027 Winter Gear Guide: more than 400 products, a SKI Test at Deer Valley, and a ski boot test on Mount Hood (50 pairs, 10 testers, two weeks).

It has been revealed that of those more than 400 products, 20 earned highest honors. Best in Test is reserved for the winners of SKI Test, our annual ski shootout at Deer Valley, where each ski goes head to head with a full category field and comes out on top. Editors’ Choice goes to gear that brought newly introduced tech that changes how well the product works, proved themselves season after season, or surprised us in a category where nobody saw it coming. Best Overall is the simplest: the product that tested better than anything else in its category.

If you’re on the hunt for latest gear this season and only the best will do, start here. Each pick links to its full roundup, where you can see how it stacks up against the competition and read the cons—we always have cons.

Sources indicate that few skis have defined a category like the Enforcer. At 99 millimeters underfoot, it’s built for skiers who attack the whole mountain, from refrozen groomers to chopped-up afternoon snow. Its heft keeps it calm where lighter skis get bounced around, and edge grip on firm snow is a standout. The tradeoff is effort: it rewards sharp technique, floats less well than its width suggests, and can feel like work in bumps. Expect a driver’s ski. Read the full review.

Women who spend more time off the groomers than on them will find a willing partner in the M-Pro W 98. At 98 millimeters, it moves between corduroy and off-piste chunder without hesitation, and its stability builds confidence when speed climbs. It’s a directional, significant-mountain-leaning ski, which means it asks for strength and a committed stance. Lighter or less aggressive skiers may find it beefy. For rippers who want one ski to charge anywhere, it delivers. Read the full women’s all-mountain ski guide.

Sources indicate that the M-Free 108 won Best in Test without winning a single performance category, a reminder that consistency beats flash. Testers found it versatile enough to cover a wide range of terrain, and it floats like a ski much wider than its 108-millimeter waist. That makes it a smart pick for freeride-minded skiers who want one pair for storm days and everything in between, rather than a specialist that shines in only one condition. Read the full review.

Where some wide skis chase fun, the Santa Ana 102 chases speed. It stays calm through chopped-up snow and meets every snow type with energy, as long as the skier can match it. That’s the catch: lesser-skilled skiers may find it unforgiving, it’s stiff in bumps, and driving it takes real leg strength. For strong skiers who want a 102-millimeter ski that rewards commitment and holds its line when the going gets tough, it’s the benchmark. Read the full review.

Industry observers note that the Mantra name has long meant power, and the 88 shrinks that formula into a frontside ski. Testers praised how smoothly it rolls from one edge to the other, with a responsiveness closer to a race ski than most frontside designs. It’s stiff and demanding, and the tip can deflect when snow gets cut up, so it’s happiest on groomed and firm terrain. Pick it if you ski fast, ski hard, and want a precise tool. Read the full review.

If you want a frontside ski that takes the guesswork out of starting a turn, the Arcade W 88 is it. A substantial tip pulls you into an arc intuitively, and it handles groomers, bumps, and mixed snow with equal composure. It wants to stay on edge, so it’s not the choice for sideways, slarvy fun. Skiers who prefer a grippy, predictable ride across changing conditions will find a trustworthy everyday partner here. Read the full review.

Sources indicate that carving skis have drifted wider and friendlier, but the Montero AX still feels like race ski’s cousin. With an 80-millimeter waist, it tips onto edge with little effort and stays planted at speed, rewarding skiers who drive it with intent. The price is steep, and less assertive skiers may find it unforgiving. If you live for corduroy and want a ski you can trust when the speedometer climbs, this is the one. Read the full review.

Sources indicate that powder skis can be lively or powerful, rarely both. The Antimatter 114 manages it. Generous rocker at the tip and tail plus a 114-millimeter waist keep it on top of deep snow, while the ski still feels energetic when you hit it hard. It’s a lot of ski for intermediates and comes only in long lengths, and a few testers noticed some wobble in a straight line at full speed. Expert-leaning powder hounds will love it. Read the full review.

Armada’s Locator 112 is a touring ski with a soft-snow personality. At 1,575 grams per ski, testers found it exceptionally playful in powder. It gives up some reliability on firm snow and isn’t the most nimble in tight terrain, so it’s best matched to substantial, open lines and storm-day objectives rather than icy couloirs. Choose it when your blueprint is untracked snow and a lively ride. Read the full review.

Industry observers note that A liner refresh, not a redesign, keeps the Shadow MV on top. It suits skiers who equate comfort with a precise, snug fit rather than extra room, with a 100-millimeter last and a progressive flex that transfers power straight to the ski. Testers liked the shin fit and flex feel, and the liner’s design helps avoid pressure points. It runs slightly short, so size carefully. Read the full review.

Tecnica’s Mach 1 is a perennial favorite in SKI’s boot tests, and the women’s TD2 version earns Editors’ Choice by being easier to live with. It’s simpler to get on than past generations, fits a broad range of foot and leg shapes, and delivers a quick, snappy flex that translates to rapid edge response. On fit: Ankle pockets may bite at first. Read the full review.

The Radical Pro is a midweight touring boot that doesn’t feel like a compromise. At 1,400 grams, it offers a remarkably free 60-degree range of motion for climbing, then stiffens progressively as you flex forward for the descent. Fit is generous through a wide last, which suits many feet but may feel cavernous on narrow ones. For backcountry skiers who need one boot to handle long approaches and confident skiing, it makes a strong case. Read the full review.

Raide’s TourTech is a shell built for people who earn their turns. It breathes well when you’re working hard on the skin track, packs down small enough to stash when the sun comes out, and carries thoughtful backcountry touches. The tradeoff of a shell is warmth: on the coldest storm days you’ll need to layer underneath. It isn’t cheap, but for women who tour more than they lap lifts, it earns its Editors’ Choice. Read the full review.

Industry observers note that fit is the whole argument for the Bigline Bib. The cut has plenty of room for puffy long underwear, but three adjustment points (waist cinches, long suspenders, hem buttons) snug it down so nothing drags or sags. A soft three-layer Pertex Shield outer reliably deflected soggy Pacific Northwest storms. Thigh pockets swallow a skin each, so slackcountry laps are covered. These are uninsulated, so be sure to layer up for cold days. Read the full review.

Sources indicate that testers had a hard time finding fault with the Chariot Primo, which is a rarity among women’s ski pants. Its hybrid fit is relaxed enough to layer and move in without getting baggy, and short, regular, and tall inseams let you skip the tailor. Three-layer PNW Primo fabric offers 20,000 millimeters of waterproofing, and TechSteel kick patches guard the cuffs. With no insulation, you’ll need to layer for the weather, but we love these bibs’ versatility. Read the full review.

According to recent reports, A former Editors’ Choice winner, the Defiant Shell takes the best all-around honor among men’s jackets on comfort, weather protection, and smart details. Venting is excellent, the pocket layout is generous, and the double front zipper is a thoughtful touch. In stormier conditions, its proprietary membrane kept wet, heavy flakes from soaking through. It’s uninsulated, so you control warmth with layers. Read the full review.

Salomon’s Skarn Prime earns the overall nod in the goggles category by doing a lot well. A toric lens gives an expansive field of view, the face foam is layered three deep, and the magnetic lens swap is quick and intuitive. It also pairs with a wide range of helmets. The catches are fit and price: it’s sized large, so smaller faces may swim in it, and $295 is steep. If it fits your face, it’s the one to beat. Read the full review.

In a recent development, sweet Protection’s Switcher 2Vi MIPS took the overall helmet title on comfort, goggle compatibility, and airflow. The Occigrip turn-dial makes fit adjustments quick, and the 2Vi platform and MIPS layer handle impact protection. Venting is excellent, which helps when the temperature climbs. The only real complaint was bulky ear pads. At 560 grams and $300, it’s not the lightest or cheapest lid, but it covers a lot of ground with few compromises. Read the full review.

According to recent reports, rab’s Guide GTX Gauntlets give you protection without bulk. A Gore-Tex Active shell keeps weather out, 100-gsm PrimaLoft Gold and a high-pile lining supply the warmth, and the low-profile cuff tucks over or under a jacket sleeve cleanly. They’re built to last through a hard season, and Rab also offers an undercuff glove and a mitten version if the gauntlet isn’t your style. At $170, they’re a smart, do-it-all pick. Read the full review.

It has been revealed that swany’s Nexus leans on a upcoming heating platform called ewool and 22-watt-hour batteries, and the result is heat that lasts: up to eight hours on low, four on normal, three on high. Testers liked the haptic feedback when changing settings, the high-quality leather, and that you can charge without pulling the batteries out. A mitt version is also offered for the coldest hands. At $480 it’s an investment, but it’s the heated glove to beat. Read the full review.

#21379. Industry News: “These Aren’t Victimless Crimes.” Vandals Deface Ancient Petroglyphs Near Moab.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (677 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: “These Aren’t Victimless Crimes.” Vandals Deface Ancient Petroglyphs Near Moab.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vandals scratched graffiti above ancient animal petroglyphs at the Bear Panel along Highway 279 near Moab, Utah.
  • The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) unveiled on November 6 that it was investigating vandalism at two ancient rock-art sites near Moab, Utah, where someone carved names into petroglyphs, leaving damage that may be impossible to remove.
  • The incidents occurred at the Bear Panel, a rock-art site along Highway 279 near the Colorado River, and another panel near Hell’s Revenge, a popular four-wheel-drive trail in the Sand Flats Recreation Area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vandals scratched graffiti above ancient animal petroglyphs at the Bear Panel along Highway 279 near Moab, Utah. (Photo: BLM Utah).

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) unveiled on November 6 that it was investigating vandalism at two ancient rock-art sites near Moab, Utah, where someone carved names into petroglyphs, leaving damage that may be impossible to remove.

The incidents occurred at the Bear Panel, a rock-art site along Highway 279 near the Colorado River, and another panel near Hell’s Revenge, a popular four-wheel-drive trail in the Sand Flats Recreation Area.

It has been revealed that “These images are a physical expression of the past, their connection to their ancestors and to that landscape,” Chris Merritt, Utah’s state historic preservation officer, told Outside. “They will now forever be scarred by someone’s thoughtlessness, and that hurts the continuation of culture.”.

The BLM has not publicly identified any suspects in the two latest incidents. An agency spokesperson told the Moab newspaper The Times-Independent that the agency planned to treat the graffiti in the days following its November 6 announcement, although some damage may be permanent.

Under the federal Archaeological Resources Protection Act, vandalizing protected archaeological sites can carry fines of up to $20,000 and two years in prison.

It has been revealed that photos show the name “Meru” scratched beside ancient carvings depicting a bear and a bighorn sheep at the Bear Panel. At the second site, near Hell’s Revenge, someone carved “Craig W” across several petroglyph figures.

According to recent reports, merritt mentioned much of the artwork at the two sites dates back roughly 1,500 years and reflects Ancestral Puebloan and Fremont traditions, along with those of more recent Indigenous communities. The panels are part of a larger cultural landscape around Moab, where Indigenous peoples once lived, farmed, and traveled, he said.

Restoring the damaged petroglyphs presents different challenges at each site, Merritt said.

In a recent development, at the site near Hell’s Revenge, vandals scratched graffiti directly across ancient carvings. Merritt noted that typical fixes, such as scrubbing the stone or trying to conceal the marks with pigments, risk damaging the original artwork underneath.

The Bear Panel presents a different problem. A crack in the sandstone just below the graffiti means that scraping the rock could create openings for rainwater, weakening the structure through freeze-thaw cycles.

“Five minutes of damage could take weeks of repair to do carefully to preserve the subsurface imagery and the rock face,” Merritt noted, emphasizing that any remediation must involve consultation with descendant tribal communities.

Merritt mentioned rock-art vandalism has become more widespread in Utah in recent years, a problem he believes is partly connected to growing visitation on public lands.

“We’ve always had folks going back to the 19th century scraping their initials on the panels, but what we’re seeing within five or six years is a pretty significant increase in the scale and distribution, hitting archaeological panels that have never had graffiti before,” Merritt stated.

The latest incidents follow another case in March 2026, when the Grand County Sheriff’s Office investigated graffiti carved into petroglyphs near Tusher Tunnel, along an off-highway vehicle route northwest of Moab.

Sources indicate that to combat the problem, Merritt stated Utah is using its Protect Our Past education campaign and a statewide network of volunteer site stewards who monitor archaeological sites. Signage and fencing can also help discourage vandalism, he said.

Recent findings suggest that in November 2025, a Utah woman who vandalized petroglyphs on BLM land near Wire Pass was sentenced to 12 months of probation and ordered to pay $14,853 in fines and restitution, according to a U.S. Department of Justice news release. She was also prohibited from entering BLM land during her probation.

Recent findings suggest that “These aren’t victimless crimes,” Merritt said. “We need to find ways to catch, prosecute, and convict these folks, so it sends a message to future visitors that this is not acceptable in Utah or anywhere you visit heritage sites.”.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Moab BLM Law Enforcement at 435-259-2131.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers.
  • “His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat mentioned.
  • Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Shah Daulat on Facebook).

It has been revealed that shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat mentioned. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”.

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

Industry observers note that but his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

In a recent development, “May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”.

In September, the artist Iowna Chichowich installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

#21377. Breaking: 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1522 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

It has been revealed that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Recent findings suggest that linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden mentioned, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

It has been revealed that linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

In a recent development, survival promptly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling initiative was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden stated. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other looks. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden stated. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

Sources indicate that when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden remarked. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

#21375. Jimmy Chin on His Latest Mount Everest Film and Latest Book

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Jimmy Chin on His Latest Mount Everest Film and Latest Book

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Chin, pictured in Joshua Tree National Park, described writing his fresh book as both a marathon and a sprint.
  • In spring 2026, Jimmy Chin flew to Nepal.
  • Together, they made their way to Everest Base Camp, stopping in the tiny villages that populate the roadless Khumbu Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jimmy Chin, pictured in Joshua Tree National Park, described writing his fresh book as both a marathon and a sprint. (Photo: Beau Grealy/Trunk Archive).

In spring 2026, Jimmy Chin flew to Nepal. It was his 15th trip to the Greater Ranges over 25 years spent on expeditions to climb and photograph its snow-covered giants. The trip was a departure from the high-octane sufferfests he’s often done, and it also marked a different type of first: the first time he brought his kids, Marina (12) and James (10), along. Showing them the mountains that have inspired him for decades, and often pulled him away from them for months at a time, was memorable for Chin.

Together, they made their way to Everest Base Camp, stopping in the tiny villages that populate the roadless Khumbu Valley. When they crawled into their tents at 17,598 feet, they were proud of themselves.

Sources indicate that outside Phortse, a small village in Sagarmatha National Park, a helicopter dropped off a special guest who’d come to say hi: Jim Morrison. Morrison hadn’t wanted to miss the kids’ first trip to Nepal, and they were shocked to see him walking toward them on the trail. In town, they went to the Khumbu Climbing Center, where Nepali climbers and high-altitude workers train to operate safely in the substantial mountains, to hang with Sherpa friends and their families, and to pick up their guide, Pemba Sherpa (Sharwa).

Twenty years earlier, Chin had encountered a then 15-year-old Pemba for the first time in that exact spot. It was just a few years after the center had opened, and he and the legendary mountaineer Conrad Anker were on the way to climb Cholatse. “I really encouraged his photography and filmmaking,” said Chin.

It turned out to be kismet: Pemba worked with Chin as a cinematographer on his film, Everest: The Other Side. Pemba was there in October 2025 documenting Jim Morrison as he made his first turn off the 29,032-foot summit. Morrison made history that day after completing a mind-boggling ski descent: an unforgiving 9,000-foot line of the North Face of Everest via the Hornbein and Japanese Couloirs.

In a recent development, chin’s team of climbers, filmmakers, and support crew added 12 newly introduced names to the short list of people who had ever summited Everest via the North Face. Ascending the route alone would’ve been enough, but Chin was there as Morrison’s climbing partner while simultaneously directing a feature film. The 53-year-old has made a career of combining high-angle endeavors with filmmaking. In 2011, he climbed the Shark’s Fin, a 4,500-foot route, alongside Anker and Renan Ozturk to film what would become the 2015 movie Meru. When Alex Honnold climbed the 3,000-foot granite prow of El Capitan in Yosemite National Park without a rope, Chin was there to capture that too. Free Solo went on to win an Academy Award.

His newest film, which was co-directed with Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and made its theatrical debut in IMAX on October 30, was built on every single one of the skills Chin has developed over his career climbing and documenting expeditions on some of the world’s most challenging peaks.

“This is kind of like the culmination of all my collective experiences as a climber and a photographer and a filmmaker and a producer and a director and all the things,” remarked Chin of making the film.

Recent findings suggest that when Chin took the last few steps to the summit of Mount Everest, his third time standing up there, he was surprised to find himself overcome with emotion. During the climb, he’d been so focused: He was thinking about breathing, consumed by the sheer physicality of climbing at altitude, busy worrying about Morrison and the team’s safety, and planning out shot lists and contingency prepares. He’d thought about every worst-case scenario, but he’d failed to consider what it would feel like to succeed. The years of hard work flashed in front of his eyes. He collapsed into Morrison’s arms, in tears.

“I looked over into Nepal and saw Makalu and Lhotse, and I mean the whole Himalaya spread out in front of me,” noted Chin. It had taken seven years to get the team up there. “Everything hit me at the same time and I totally fell apart.”.

While he felt a substantial weight lift from his shoulders after getting everyone up and down Everest safely, he still felt the enormous weight of having two of his closest friends, Morrison and Morrison’s late partner Hilaree Nelson, entrust him with their story. He’d met Nelson 20 years earlier when they both joined the athlete team at The North Face at the same time. He knew he had to get it right.

According to recent reports, after six years of working on the film, Chin and producer Shannon Dill traveled to Tahoe City last June to show Morrison a rough cut. When it was over, there was a lot of emotion in the room, and people were crying. Morrison got up and walked to the back of the theater to wrap Chin in a massive hug.

Industry observers note that during the final phases of editing the film, Chin was also working on a deadline to finish his latest book, Rules to Live By. “I had like three months of 16-hour days, seven days a week,” he said. “When people say it’s a marathon, not a sprint, I was like, ‘This is both.’”.

For the book, Chin interviewed ten people he looks up to, from Lynsey Addario to Simone Biles to Yo-Yo Ma, all of whom have helped shape the way he thinks about what really matters in life.

Both Bill King and Ridley Scott talked to him about honesty, and it’s stuck with him. “You have to tell the truth,” he noted. “It’s hard to do, but you have to do it, and you have to do it early because it only becomes harder.” Telling the truth is like training a muscle, he said, and exercising it becomes easier with practice and, with enough time, just becomes how you naturally operate. We’ve all had an experience that would’ve been easier if we’d just been honest up front, said Chin.

He draws inspiration from actress Annette Bening and how she leads: quietly, in a way that embodies the Daoist idea that the greatest leaders are the ones that no one knows are leading. “She makes people feel seen and heard, and when she walks on set, people will do anything for this woman because they want to,” he said. “I was really paying attention to how she moved through the world. It’s about listening to people and making people feel heard.”.

Years after Pemba met Chin, he started working on climbing expeditions, following in his father’s footsteps. His dad bought him a Lumix digital camera to take with him on his first expedition to Mount Everest. On the summit, he snapped a few photos.

In a recent development, when Meru came out, Pemba remembers feeling deeply inspired by Chin’s work. He could not have imagined that a decade later, after years spent working in the mountains and honing his craft, he would find himself filming for Chin’s production, with his camera aimed at Chin during the emotional moments that transpired on the summit before Morrison’s ski.

Chin has spent much of his life forging his own path in the mountains, making daring first ascents and ski descents, but has since shifted his focus toward giving opportunities to the next generation coming up behind him. When a significant objective is on the horizon, he makes sure to bring new faces along.

“Jimmy is a substantial influence on me, and a big mentor,” mentioned Pemba. “Experiencing a climb with the man himself and working for the man himself? Yeah, it was really an honor.”.

Industry observers note that hoping to buy a gift for an ultralight hiker? Here’s the hard truth: Whatever you purchase will be weighed, then quietly stuffed in a closet. I know, because after a decade of thru-hiking, I’ve almost completely wallpapered my small room with all the copies of Wild I’ve been given. Thank you, but please stop.

Apart from heavy gifts, the last thing an ultralight hiker needs is someone else choosing their massive three. The little things, though? That’s where a good gift can surprise them. This year’s picks tackle ten small annoyances of life on trail, from a rigid bottle that actually works with a filter to a sun glove that doesn’t plaster to your hands.

Recent findings suggest that single-use bottles crease, crinkle, and need replacing, but my original ThruBottle survived 1,800 miles this summer with plenty of life left. My only gripe was that it was too stiff to squeeze water through a filter. I’ve upgraded to the upcoming ThruBottle 1000, which has a softer body and sheds nearly an ounce, weighing 2.2 ounces for a full liter.

The zip-lock bag you’d rather no one ever rummaged through has a 0.14-ounce alternative: this cap turns a compatible 28 mm bottle into a portable bidet. I find that it works best with a squeezable bottle. Unlike TP, it never runs out halfway through a section.

In a recent development, I sleep cold, and when the temperature drops on the trail, my ears and neck are often the first places I want extra warmth. The Shag Hood, made from Polartec Alpha Direct, covers them for 1.16 ounces, so I can skip carrying another full layer. Bonus: It’s gorpcore enough to wear off trail too.

My old half-finger sun gloves always came off inside out, and getting them back on over sweaty hands was a nightmare. The éclipse gloves have a thumb hole and mitten-style opening, so they slide on and off. They weigh 0.35 ounces and give me UPF 50+ sun protection on the backs of my hands, where multiple rounds of sunscreen have never been enough.

Recent findings suggest that A camera buried in your pack takes no photos. The three-ounce Capture Clip attaches to a shoulder strap or belt, so I can grab my camera when the light is just right, instead of getting stuck crouching over my pack, still fumbling for it when the light’s gone.

Sources indicate that the long handle keeps your knuckles out of dinner at the bottom of a freeze-dried meal bag. The 0.8-ounce titanium spork would outlast my hiking career if I could stop losing it. I found four on my last thru-hike, so I’m clearly not the only one.

It has been revealed that A half-empty fuel canister is too precious to toss but annoying to carry. I’ve envied hikers using heavier transfer valves, but couldn’t justify the weight until the Alpenflow dropped. It weighs 0.09 ounces and transfers leftover fuel between two standard EN417 canisters, including those from MSR, Jetboil, and Snow Peak.

According to recent reports, leukotape is my holy grail bandage. It stays on through sweat, mud, and sketchy river crossings, and I’ve accidentally left a strip on for weeks. It’s gotten harder for me to find it in stores lately, so a spare roll is a keeper. I wrap a generous amount around my trekking poles instead of carrying the full 3.9-ounce roll.

For 10,000 thru-hiking miles, my pillow was the head of my dirty air mattress propped up on a water bottle, which rolled out from under me all night. Don’t make my mistake. For 1.9 ounces, the regular size is the real deal, and it packs down to the size of a pool ball. Pricey for a pillow, but I sleep better.

This 0.11-ounce Dyneema pouch stops loose tent stakes from rattling around in your pack. You don’t think you need one until a rogue stake starts working its way through your bug netting. Not that I, a seasoned professional and expert patcher, know anything about that.

The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels.
  • Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect.
  • In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson).

Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

According to recent reports, as someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

Recent findings suggest that if you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

According to recent reports, I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, Latest Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

The “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

Sources indicate that norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.

Industry News: Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • According to recent reports, diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

According to recent reports, diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

Recent findings suggest that this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

In a recent development, jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Sources indicate that having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really major for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

According to recent reports, I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a big thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making upcoming friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

According to recent reports, no, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite promptly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Industry observers note that now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

In a recent development, at the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

Patagonia Storm Shift Jacket – Men's.

Helly Hansen Unisex Odin Winter Gloves.

Hardcore skiers can be difficult to shop for.

Recent findings suggest that the more involved you become as a skier, the more specific your wants and needs get. Suddenly, the standard goggles no longer apply, and you choose your jacket not based on what looks cool but on what functions in the ways you need. If you have a dedicated skier in your life, it’s not always obvious what to gift them, especially since you’ll want them to use it and love it.

According to recent reports, to help ease your mind, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite gift ideas for the people in our lives who eat, sleep, and breathe skiing: from powderhounds to corduroy snobs, this list has a little something for everyone. And we can guarantee it—we’re somewhat of ski hardos ourselves.

We all have that one friend who complains a little too much about being cold. But when your butt freezes the second you sit on the lift, can you blame them? That’s where insulated knickers come in. Throw them on over your base layers for extra protection your derrière didn’t know it needed. Wear them over your base layer for some extra warmth or on their own for a more loose-fitting base under your ski pants. These are the perfect gift for the skier you know who likes to get a lot of days in and stay nice and toasty on the hill. —Giorgia Menetre, Senior Social Media Strategist.

According to recent reports, good goggles don’t need to cost a fortune. Dependable click-in, click-out interchangeable lenses are a staple for a reason—they’ll get you through just about every condition. Smith’s OG reliable goggles offer a wide field of vision, ChromaPop lenses that make the view pop, and a flexible, comfortable frame. Lenses swap easily, with no worry of a magnetic slip-up. Don’t let another ski day go by letting the skier you love squint through bad light. —GM.

It has been revealed that these booties come with a high price tag, but they’ll be the gift hardcore skiers never forget. This updated compression boot from Normatec takes the pressurized, full-length boot system that has proven recovery patterns and adds heat. Dynamic air circulation throughout the boot’s treatment session helps muscles recover faster and reduces soreness. Remember how good it feels to put an achy and tired calf next to a hot tub jet? Now, imagine that level of recovery from the comfort of your couch. Boots come in three sizes and can fit a wide range of heights.

Sources indicate that please note that boots will ship the week of 11/23. —Jamie Aranoff, SKI Senior Editor.

Industry observers note that hestra’s Fall Line mittens are consistently ranked as some of the warmest by our testers. The mittens have a cozy inner layer of brushed polyester and foam to keep hands insulated without overheating. The outside is leather that, once broken in, is soft and dexterous. Wrist straps ensure that the mittens stay with the skier, and not at the bottom of a chairlift. The mittens are on the pricier side, but will surely be a gift that skiers cherish for years. The same warmth also comes in a glove. —JA.

Read our full review and browse other warm gloves and mittens here.

Recent findings suggest that vests are underrated heroes for skiers: they’re a great midlayer for touring and warmer days, easy to layer, and stylish enough to wear around. The Helium Utility down vest from Peak Performance checks all three of these boxes and more. The vest is incredibly lightweight and packs down into its pocket. More importantly, it’s windproof and water-repellent. A cinch at the bottom allows for customization for the right fit. —JA.

If you’ve got an impossible-to-shop-for skier on your list, then look no further: this adventure camera from Nocs Provisions (yes, the same brand that makes binoculars) is sure to please. The camera is incredibly easy to use, even with thick gloves or mittens. Its simple one-button technology allows skiers to easily whip it out of a pocket and hit record (it takes both photos and videos). There’s no SD card needed, and content is easy to transfer to either a phone or computer with cords included. The camera takes retro-style photos and videos and comes with a lifetime “no matter what” policy. —JA.

For any serious skier, Dermatone chapstick is the ultimate stocking stuffer. Not only will Dermatone protect lips from chapping, but the SPF keeps skin from burning. It also belongs in every first aid kit; it’s proven to help stop frostbite on extremities like lips, noses, and cheeks. Most ski resorts sell Dermatone somewhere in the shop, but here’s your chance to stock up and avoid inflated prices. Your lips, nose, cheeks, and just about everywhere else will thank you. —JA.

Fleeces are always a solid gift, but Ridge Merino’s Alpha Wool Insulated jacket goes the extra mile. This fleece is designed to act as an outer layer for warmer days or uphilling, and a midlayer for when temperatures drop. What makes this fleece different is a mix of strategically placed wool to wick away moisture in places you sweat most, matched with a water-resistant Pertex Quantum Air that acts more like a shell than a fleece. The fleece is complete with a hood, so no matter the weather, you’ll be prepared.—JA.

The North Face just inked a deal with U.S. Ski & Snowboard to outfit the men’s and women’s alpine and freestyle teams for the next eight years. Bonus: They just released a version of the kit for the skiing public. The Comp Team Gore-Tex 2L Freeride and 3L Alpine jackets and pants come in alpine and freestyle designs, but the tech is the same: fully wind- and waterproof with plenty of features such as helmet-compatible hoods,  pit and thigh zips, and a multitude of smartly placed pockets. Don’t forget about the U.S. Ski Team crest on the right chest and all of the relevant sponsor badges to complete the look for your U.S. Ski Team superfan. —Samantha Berman, SKI Executive Editor.

According to recent reports, here’s the perfect stocking stuffer for the uphiller on your list—or anyone who wants to add a little flair to their kit. Skida’s Pursuit Headband features the new Alpenbloom print, designed by U.S. Ski Teamer Paula Moltzan as part of the brand’s 2026–’27 collaboration with U.S. Ski & Snowboard. Beyond the athlete-designed pattern, the headband is a genuinely useful piece, made with a moisture-wicking, quick-drying fabric that regulates temperature without trapping too much heat and cozy fleece lining for comfort. A secure, nonslip fit keeps it in place whether you’re skiing, skinning, or working up a sweat on a cold-weather run. For guys, check out Ryan Cochran-Siegle’s Under the Lights print, which comes in a hat and a neckwarmer in addition to a headband.—SB.

In a recent development, the Black Diamond Spark Mitts have been a tester favorite for years, and for good reason: you can’t go wrong with a short gauntlet mitt with a full leather outer. But the Spark goes beyond boring old performance. Every few seasons, Black Diamond drops a colorway with a fun, embroidered design on the inner side of the index finger. The Angel Collinson mustache model was our longtime favorite, but the current model with shark teeth is just as fun—and a good reminder that skiing isn’t so serious. —Jenny Wiegand, Outside Associate Gear Director.

For the skier who skis in all conditions, this is the midlayer to give. At just 9.8 ounces, the Lightstream Full Zip stays unbulky while delivering serious warmth from -10 to 50 degrees. Vivo Extreme insulation is zoned for the job: 60 grams in the body and collar, 40 in the hood and sleeves, and 25 in the underarms and side seams. The 15-denier stretch nylon/PU ripstop shell is tough enough for daily abuse, and it also works as an outer layer for fall bike commutes and dog walks. Pair it with the Lightstream Insulated Short, made for skiers who run cold but won’t give up their shell pants, even on resort days. Full-length side zips let you take the shorts off when things heat up, without removing your ski pants. Light and packable, they’re also the ultimate emergency layer to stash in your boot bag. Available for men and women. —JW.

According to recent reports, carv is the perfect gift for the skier who has everything, mostly because it’s the kind of gadget they’d struggle to justify buying for themselves. But if someone gave it to them? Game on. I’ll admit, I was skeptical of this digital ski coach, which uses sensors attached to your boots to analyze your technique and deliver real-time feedback. But after a few seasons, I’m hooked. It turns improving your skiing into a game, and it’s surprisingly addictive. Ted Ligety once told me his secret to topping the Carv leaderboard: find a stretch of groomer where you can make 10 perfect turns, then ski it over and over until you top the leaderboard. Personally, I might get distracted looking for powder, but I’ve found Carv makes even an ordinary groomer day more interesting. It’s fun, genuinely useful, and exactly the sort of gift someone might not know they wanted. Editor’s note: The list price includes a 12-month membership; continued coaching requires renewal. —Sierra Shafer, Editorial Director, Lifestyle.

In a recent development, few things in skiing are more universally useful than a Voilé Strap. These simple, stretchy polyurethane straps are the duct tape of the ski world, minus the sticky residue. Recent findings suggest that why do we organize entire lives around sliding down snowy mountains?
