Alex Honnold, holding a bowl of Cheerios in one hand and a spoon of peanut butter in the other, stands at a kitchen island between his two giggling daughters and scowls at the clock. Here it is, barely 8 A.M., and he is already running late. Honnold rapidly calculates the jam-packed agenda for what will be his family’s final summer day at their vacation cabin in South Lake Tahoe. Valuable seconds tick by.

After breakfast, Honnold must drop the girls off at preschool and then link up with a team of photographers and videographers at Pie Shop, a climbing crag on the other side of town. There, he will pose for a magazine cover shoot while clinging to rotund granite boulders, before speeding back to the cabin to have lunch with his aunt, who is visiting from Idaho. After that, Honnold will pack his luggage for an upcoming family trip to Italy. Finally, the Honnolds will host a few friends and neighbors for a goodbye barbecue.

The breakneck schedule is made more challenging by lingering jet lag from a recent trip to London, where Honnold delivered a motivational speech at an event hosted by his longtime sponsor the North Face.

“These days I feel like a ping-pong ball,” Honnold indicates. More seconds tick by.

Honnold will have to complete much of today’s agenda while answering the prying questions of a pesky journalist—me. Back in January, Honnold’s Netflix special Skyscraper Live thrust him into millions of living rooms across the planet, elevating him to a loftier stratosphere of fame. At Outside, we named Honnold an Outsider of the Year, in part, for bringing the grandeur of climbing to such a massive audience. Now, I have traveled to the Honnold family cabin to examine how a sudden spike in stardom is impacting outdoor recreation’s biggest celebrity.

Industry observers note that how’s he coping? Well enough, I’d say, but boy does he seem exhausted. A coffee might help, but he still doesn’t touch the stuff. Honnold rubs his forehead. I notice more than a few streaks of gray dotting the sides of his close-cropped hair. Creases run across his cheeks, and deep crow’s-feet flare from both eyes. He yawns as he presents the bowl of cereal to June, who frowns. Sanni McCandless Honnold, his wife of six years, reaches over the sink to deliver Cheerios to Alice, who everyone calls Summer. There’s more giggling. McCandless Honnold presents each child with outfit options for the day. Red dress, yellow, or green? Definitely green.

In a recent development, remembering his own wardrobe choices for the upcoming photo shoot, Honnold lumbers down the hallway toward the garage, which houses indoor climbing walls, free weights, and exercise equipment. He grabs several North Face shirts. Red or green? Definitely red. Back in the kitchen, a spoon clatters to the floor. The pitter-patter of approaching feet echoes from the hallway, and in a flash, the kiddos burst into the gym. Breakfast is over.

Industry observers note that june, the elder of the two, grabs a gymnastics ring dangling from the ceiling and begins to twirl. Summer crouches on the padded floor and watches her sister.

Industry observers note that “Yesterday was classic,” Honnold tells me later. “I woke up really early so I could do my gym workout before everyone got up. Somehow the babies heard me and woke up too and came in right when I was in the middle of everything.”.

According to recent reports, honnold pauses before delivering a playful imitation of his wife. “Sanni is like, ‘You’re finally home from your London trip and all you want to do is climb?’’’.

All you want to do is climb? may seem like an odd question for the world’s most famous rock climber. But these days, scaling rock is just one of the many tasks on Honnold’s daily agenda. In the wake of Skyscraper Live, Honnold’s life has become a dizzying array of paid speaking engagements, sponsor meet-and-greets, recording segments for his two podcasts Climbing Gold and Planet Visionaries, video shoots for his Outside TV show Out There with Alex Honnold, and other media hits. He graciously agrees to a high percentage of these interviews—yes, including Outside—which leads to an impossibly tight schedule.

It has been revealed that he also has family commitments: dropping his daughters off at school, feeding them, and the usual weekend outings to playdates and playgrounds. In casual conversation, Honnold affectionately refers to his daughters as “the babies,” even though June is 4 and Summer is 2.

Recent findings suggest that “The babies were harder this summer than last year,” Honnold says. He recounts a recent backpacking trip that sounds familiar to anyone who has attempted to adventure with small children. There was crying, smiles, ups, and downs. In total, the family covered just a few miles over the course of two days.

“You get those moments where it feels wholesome and fun and everything is cute,” Honnold states. “And other times when it feels like a tremendous amount of labor. I suspect that, for me, the best times are still ahead.”.

So, back to rock climbing. Alas, it’s a somewhat touchy subject. On many days, climbing is an activity that Honnold squeezes in, pounds out, or cuts short. Daylong ascents of gleaming granite are often replaced by two-hour sweat sessions in his home gym. Honnold admits it is not what he predicted he’d be doing at age 40.

It has been revealed that “This year I can count on one hand the number of times I’ve really been proud of something I’ve climbed on rock,” Honnold says. “The frustration of sucking is the essence of middle age.”.

Honnold pauses before laughing. “Middle age is the ratio of how often you fall below your expectations, compared to how often you surpass them,” he adds. “Unfortunately, my standards for my climbing haven’t shrunk. I think it would be easier if they had.”.

In a recent development, it’s well past go-time, and Honnold leads the charge toward his green Rivian SUV waiting out front. I snatch the middle seat in the back, flanked on each side by the girls in their car seats. Today, breakfast will be finished on the way to school. McCandless Honnold hands out fruit pouches. The girls squeal with glee.

There are hugs, kisses, and see-you-soons, and Honnold drives out onto the main road, toward preschool, Pie Shop, and what will be a serene afternoon in the Sierra Nevada. I process the whirlwind morning: the chaos, crunched schedule, spilled cereal, and Honnold’s occasionally futile pursuit of outdoor time. It’s all so much to take in, and yet, it feels so incredibly familiar. It’s the grind that millions of outdoors-loving moms and dads, myself included, live every day. We squeeze in that hike, that bike ride, that jog in between Zoom meetings and school pickups. We do so knowing that we’ll never quite be as fast or as strong as we were in our twenties, when our carefree lives afforded us the freedom to play outdoors all day, day after day, with zero consequences.

According to recent reports, honnold is one of us now, I conclude. Ever since Honnold burst into the mainstream consciousness with his death-defying free solo ascents, journalists—including yours truly—have sought to explain why he is so different from the average person. Now, at age 40, he is a Netflix star, a millionaire, and at the absolute zenith of his popularity. And yet, Alex Honnold is potentially more like us than at any point in his life.

Recent findings suggest that honnold has now been part of our lives for the better part of two decades. The iconic image of him tiptoeing across Thank God Ledge on the face of Half Dome graced the cover of National Geographic way back in September of 2011. The 60 Minutes profile of Honnold, with footage of him free soloing the Sentinel in Yosemite, beamed to TV audiences a month later. His memoir, Alone on the Wall, came out in 2015. Industry observers note that “That explanation has always felt off to me,” Honnold notes when I present it to him. “I know I might be an unusual person, but I’ve taken a lot of tests, and I’m pretty sure I’m not on the spectrum.”.

In a recent development, in a 2016 story for Nautilus, Honnold subjected himself to a bizarre psychological test, in which neuroscientists indicated him photographs of gruesome or scary images and then placed him in an MRI machine to study his amygdala, the part of the brain that supposedly triggers a fear response. The scans seemed to confirm that Honnold’s brain responds less to fear than the average person. But a decade after the test, Honnold isn’t convinced that his ability to free solo is just the byproduct of some biological quirk.

In a recent development, “People always want simple explanations for anything that seems out of the ordinary. If someone sees an exceptional athletic performance, or something that seems different, they want to know that the person doing it is different,” Honnold notes. “And, you know, the obvious explanation that it’s the product of lots of hard work and years of practice is just unsatisfactory. Because who the heck wants to dedicate their entire lives to doing that?”.

“It’s just so much easier to say, ‘That guy is weird,’” he adds.

Recent findings suggest that honnold is unwavering in explaining the root of his superpower. For 25 or so years, climbing rock consumed every waking hour of his life. Unencumbered by preschool drop-offs or honey-do lists, he threw himself at major walls in Yosemite and abroad, climbing hundreds of days each year, year after year. His physical gifts helped him surpass his peers on the toughest ascents.

According to recent reports, was he ever scared? You bet—almost every day, he notes. But, while clinging to the side of cliffs thousands of times over, Honnold found ways to silence his fear.

According to recent reports, so, which explanation is more accurate: cerebral oddity or hard work? Longtime climber and film producer Cedar Wright, who has climbed with Honnold for two decades, notes it’s closer to the latter—with an vital caveat. Honnold chose to pursue free soloing, while most people—heck, most climbers—think it’s insane.

“He and myself and the small group of free soloists out there were of the mindset that soloing really matters, and is worth the risk,” Wright said. “A lot of really good climbers, like Tommy Caldwell or Adam Ondra, want nothing to do with it. But to us, the most badass thing you can do is climb without a rope. You kind of have to believe that if you want to keep going with it.”.

In a recent development, this singular focus created, shall we call it, a relatability gap between Honnold and John Q. Public. Most stories about Honnold from his twenties and thirties mentioned that he ate and slept and filled Gatorade bottles with his own urine inside a 2002 Ford Econoline van. And in interviews from this era, Honnold comes across as, at best, robotic. At worst, an alien from another planet.

Sources indicate that but the oddball lifestyle is ultimately what propelled him to National Geographic, the Academy Awards, and into our consciousness. Wright climbed with Honnold during the mid-aughts, when they were both dirtbags living in Yosemite. Even amongst his peers, Honnold stood out because of his utter love of climbing.

Sources indicate that “There was a point when literally nobody on the planet was climbing more than Honnold, in terms of sheer volume and days in a row on rock,” Wright stated. “The guy was on a whole different level of dedication and focus.”.

Recent findings suggest that alas, those days are now long in the rearview. While Honnold’s motivation and passion and talent for climbing remain, the free time to climb every single day, day after day, has vanished, squashed by his many commitments. This tension is at the heart of Alex Honnold’s life in 2026.

The Rivian zips across South Lake Tahoe as Honnold points out landmarks. We pass a road that leads to Lover’s Leap, the local 600-foot wall where Honnold made some of his first free solo climbs in his early twenties. On the horizon sits Mount Tallac, where Honnold was saved by backcountry rescuers after he slipped and fell down a couloir when he was a teenager.

As kids, Honnold and his older sister, Stasia, spent summers at the vacation cabin in South Lake Tahoe. There were camping trips, baseball games, and afternoons spent at the nearby beach—usually with no parents in sight. The cabin also represents an eternal connection to Honnold’s father, Charles, who died of a sudden heart attack in July 2004, when Honnold was 19. Charles’ father built the cabin in a gated community a few hundred yards from the California/Nevada state line. Now, Honnold claims, going to the cabin brings up memories of his dad.

Sources indicate that “In some ways I feel his loss more now than when I was 19,” he says. “I realize that my kids never got to meet their grandfather. And he would have been fucking awesome with them. He’d probably be retired by now and would want to spend all summer here with the two of them.”.

The Honnold family cabin is key for other reasons, too. On days when the Zoom calls are few and the indoor gym has grown stale, Honnold can bolt from the cabin to breathe fresh air, climb on rock, or push his body on a trail, while still making it back for dinnertime. Honnold’s handful of 2026 outings have included more than a few local hot spots: Space Invaders, Eagle Lake Buttress, and the Tahoe Triple Crown, a punishing 18-mile out-and-back up three high peaks.

Recent findings suggest that “You have to do hundreds of climbs like these to feel like you’ve done something epic,” Honnold says. “That’s what it takes for me to feel normal these days. You can’t be a real climber if you don’t climb rock.”.

It has been revealed that of course, in true Honnold fashion, these short outings are often high-octane sufferfests that would cripple even a seasoned climber. And Honnold will push himself past the limits that most of us require for sleep and recovery in order to squeeze in an epic day. In the summer of 2025 in South Lake Tahoe, Honnold made regular outings to The Incredible Hulk, a 2,000-foot vertical wall in California’s Sawtooth Ridge, with routes rated up to 5.13. The trailhead is a two-hour drive from the family cabin, so Honnold would wake up at 2 A.M. in order to complete the round trip and be home for dinner. Longtime friend Chris Weidner would sometimes call Honnold on the phone during the drives to and from the spire for a friendly chat.

Industry observers note that “It was such a crazy schedule—for most of us, doing that climb fresh would be extremely challenging, and here he is doing it after hard days of climbing in his home gym,” Weidner remarked. “Yes, he is very committed to his family, but his intense drive and relentless need for climbing volume is still the same.”.

And climbing still provides Honnold with an emotional salve, much as it did when he was in his twenties. In the 2015 book, Alone on the Wall, Honnold described soloing the 5.12b Rainbow Wall in Nevada’s Red Rock Canyon, and how the ascent helped him work through a relationship that was not going well.

In a recent development, I ask if he still seeks out tough climbs to help process the frustration of middle-aged life. Honnold shrugs.

“I actually have a healthier approach to that type of thing now than when I was younger, because I would basically channel my inner angst to do climbs I was proud of,” he says. “It almost became a process, because I’d have to harness those moments of peak feeling to do a climb I cared about. I eventually realized I can just go out and climb the same way, without the angst.”.

Honnold adds, “Being in a committed and healthy relationship for ten years also helps.”.

But there are still times when Honnold’s emotions and his climbing intertwine. He recounts the story of a recent free solo gone wrong near the family’s full-time home in Las Vegas.

“For whatever reason, I was upset about something. Home life was hard, whatever, kids and stress,” Honnold indicates. “So, in the middle of the afternoon, I’m like, ‘Fuck it, I’m going soloing’ as a reason to get out of the house.”.

It has been revealed that but alas, there was a high-wind advisory in Vegas. The smart thing to do was to climb indoors, but Honnold was undeterred. He drove to Black Velvet Canyon trailhead in Red Rock Canyon and pointed himself up a towering route. He began free soloing a wall rated 5.10d—impossibly dangerous for most climbers without a rope—and soon realized that conditions were less than optimal.

Industry observers note that “I’m up there just getting hammered by the wind. It’s insane,” Honnold notes. “And I turn the corner and all of a sudden this huge gust, this updraft, blows chalk in my face, and the gusts are even harder, and I’m on a prow in the center of this 2,000-foot rock face.”.

A gust billowed up Honnold’s shorts and knocked his iPhone out of his pocket. The device tumbled hundreds of feet to the valley floor, breaking on impact. The phone is the only car key for Honnold’s Rivian SUV, which was also parked at the foot of the cliff. He didn’t have enough daylight to summit the climb and then hike back down. Instead, he downclimbed the wall’s 16 pitches without a rope—a sketchy undertaking. He eventually found the shattered device in the sand. Miraculously, it still turned the car on.

Industry observers note that “The next day I’m at the Apple Store buying a upcoming phone and it hits me, what an idiot I was,’’ Honnold claims. “I was like, ‘I should have just gone on a jog or something.’”.

Sources indicate that the whole ordeal sounds horrifying. But Honnold laughs and grins as he recounts the memory.

Gym time, dad adventures, and the occasional death-defying free solo simply hold Honnold over through the busiest part of the year: the spring and summer. Every fall, he carves out two weeks or so for a hard-charging adventure on rock. In 2025, he spent two weeks in Yosemite, where he and Tommy Caldwell completed a free ascent of the Platinum Wall on El Capitan, among other hard climbs. In August 2026, Honnold will spend two weeks in Europe, completing ascents on the Eiger, Matterhorn, and tough rock walls in the Dolomites.

I ask Honnold if his relationship with climbing has changed at all, now that it’s something he has to schedule into his complicated lifestyle.

According to recent reports, “In some ways, climbing is like my only opportunity to feel like I’m good at something,” he says. Being a celebrity, a paid speaker, and even a parent, Honnold admits, doesn’t always come easily. “With parenting, especially, it’s like you always feel like you’re bad at it. You know what I mean?” he adds.

Industry observers note that it’s something I know all too well. I then ask Honnold if, at age 40, he’s just as good at rock climbing as at any point in his twenties or thirties.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m probably a better climber today, in some ways, than I’ve ever been,” Honnold notes. “I’m probably stronger than I was at age 30. I suspect I could do most of the climbs that I’ve ever done, if I had the time to do them again.”.

According to recent reports, every 40-year-old weekend warrior can relate. If I only had the time. Honnold shrugs and takes it all in. He’s philosophical about the push and pull of middle age. And he tells me that, in so many words, this phase of life, with the kids, the commitments, the schedule, was, to a degree, planned. It’s the life that he and McCandless Honnold sought for themselves when they became a couple a decade ago.

“Yeah, I’ve probably given up some of my best years of climbing,” he says. “Some doors open, others close. But it was always part of our blueprint.”.

Recent findings suggest that honnold didn’t develop this adult mindset overnight, of course. The journey from van-dwelling dirtbag to committed father capable of prioritizing family and career over recreation took time and effort. And it hasn’t always been easy, Sanni McCandless Honnold tells me.

“I think, like anyone, he misses the freedom of having all the time in the world and no responsibilities, and not having to juggle the complexities of his life,” she says. “And at the same time, I don’t think he’d go back to that life.”.

McCandless Honnold, 34, met Honnold at a book signing in 2016 in Seattle, and the two quickly became a couple, traveling to climbing trips in Europe and California together. When directors began filming Free Solo six months later, they chronicled the early stages of their relationship, and captured the tension of how Honnold’s lifestyle—you know, the van and all of that climbing—collided with the requirements of partnership.

Sources indicate that some outdoor athletes never grow out of a lifestyle that prioritizes daily doses of adrenaline and adventure. But Honnold has, she says, even if he’s had to work at it. “Alex doesn’t suffer from the Peter Pan syndrome that I’ve seen a lot of adventurous people have,” she says. “Even back then, he had the ability to see his life longterm, like, ‘Yeah, I’ll probably get married and have kids. I want to provide for my family.’”.

Industry observers note that the first turning point in this evolution, McCandless Honnold indicates, occurred immediately after Free Solo. Honnold had spent years scouting El Capitan for the ascent, and then months meticulously preparing for the climb. When it was over, she says, he faced a big question: What’s next? The answer included marriage, buying a house, and traveling around the world to speak about the film to audiences.

Industry observers note that another major turn occurred in 2022 after the birth of June. McCandless Honnold underwent an emergency cesarean section, and June spent time hooked up to a ventilator in the intensive care unit. Perhaps the biggest turning point, she notes, happened in 2024, when Summer was born. McCandless Honnold suffered a painful infection just after delivery and did two stints in intensive care. Then, several weeks after returning home, she fell and broke her elbows and spent more time in the hospital.

In a recent development, “I handed him a two-week-old and a two-year-old, and he went home without Mom,” she claims. “It was one of those periods in life where you have to learn ruthless prioritization.”.

It has been revealed that over the course of several months, Honnold molded his life around the needs of the kids, staying up late to mix formula, waking up early to change diapers, and sacrificing workouts to keep his wife off her feet. Months turned into years, and as McCandless Honnold explains, Honnold learned how to juggle the many demands in his life in a way that didn’t put the entire burden of child rearing on her shoulders.

He also underwent a period of emotional growth, she says, progressing from a left-brained rationalist into a person capable of acknowledging and understanding the feelings of others. The antithesis of a robot, she assures me.

“He was never emotionless; he was never a robot,” she says. “He’s now more willing to communicate his feelings and to engage with the feelings of others.”.

Sources indicate that when I present this question to Honnold (Are you more empathetic now than you were at age 20?), he shrugs and delivers a hard no. “I’ve always understood what people are thinking, or why they’re thinking it, even if I don’t always care all that much,” he says.

In a recent development, but others in his life disagree. Weidner, who has climbed with Honnold for more than two decades, said he often suffered the wrath of Honnold’s impatience early in his career. Honnold was a better climber, and would chide Weidner when he took too long to ascend a pitch.

In the fall of 2025, the two reconnected for an ascent of the Middle Cathedral Rock in Yosemite, and Weidner noticed a major shift in Honnold’s vibe.

Recent findings suggest that “He used to be like, ‘C’mon dude, it’s only 5.12, what’s your problem?’” Weidner says. “Now he is a lot more willing to be a kind and patient climbing partner. Instead of scolding me, it’s more like, ‘C’mon Chrissy-Poo, I’m ready to climb again.’”.

It has been revealed that maybe getting older isn’t that bad. Still, Honnold’s balancing act between climbing and middle-aged life is ever-present, and every few months brings a latest wrinkle for the Honnold family to navigate. McCandless Honnold spent much of 2026 writing her first book, a self-help title called Mosaic Theory: How to Craft a Life of Many Summits. She says that, as her own ambitions and career have grown, Honnold has had to take on more family responsibilities.

Sources indicate that thus, in some ways, they were prepared for the dramatic increase in non-climbing opportunities that came Honnold’s way after Skyscraper Live beamed across Netflix. In the weeks afterward, requests for interviews and engagement poured in from all corners of the globe.

In a recent development, but in other ways, Skyscraper Live changed Honnold’s life in ways he was not prepared for—something I witness as he pulls up to the girls’ school on the western corner of South Lake Tahoe. Honnold helps his daughters walk up to the cute green building, and then briskly strolls back to the Rivian. Just as he’s about to reach the car, an enthusiastic passerby stops him, extends his hand, and begins talking. Honnold smiles and nods as he casts a few nervous glances at his watch.

Industry observers note that “Going out in public has gotten harder,” Honnold says after getting back to the car. “Fan sightings happen all the time now. I’m still not used to it.”.

Industry observers note that it used to be that only other climbers or outdoor rec aficionados would stop him for a handshake or a photo. After Skyscraper Live, it’s everyone. “Every once in a while, you’re like, ‘Did I make the wrong choice? Did I botch this whole thing? Should I still be living alone in my van?’” Honnold notes. He laughs. “And the obvious answer is no, because I don’t want to be a 65-year-old guy living in my van alone.”.

It has been revealed that honnold did not foresee the changes to his life when he summited the metal spire atop Taipei 101 and waved to the tens of thousands of awestruck onlookers below. Like free soloing El Capitan, ascending Taipei 101 was the finish line of a years-long process. Honnold first had the idea to climb a building live on television in 2013. The following year, he worked with National Geographic on the idea, eventually homing in on Taipei 101, which at the time was the world’s fourth-tallest building. But the project fell apart when the media empire learned the cost of staging the stunt.

But Honnold never forgot about the crazy idea. After the pandemic, he began working with UK production firm Plimsoll Studios, eventually filming two successful adventure series: Arctic Ascent and The Devil’s Climb. The company’s head of adventure filmmaking, James Smith, told me that Honnold frequently brought up the skyscraper idea during pitch sessions.

“Alex and I end up spending a lot of time together in these remote places,” Smith told me. “And ever since I’ve known him, he has mentioned the idea of climbing a skyscraper on TV.”.

Honnold and Smith connected for a preparatory meeting about the project in 2023, and the following year Smith traveled to Los Angeles to present the ideas to producers at Netflix. Netflix bought the idea, but Smith’s work wasn’t done—they had to choose a building. By 2023, Taipei 101 was no longer one of the world’s top-ten tallest skyscrapers. Once they winnowed the group down to four, Smith reached out to see if they could have access.

After months of outreach, Taipei 101 emerged as the final choice. Then, Smith had to figure out how to film the climb in a way that would make it compelling to the masses. His plan involved a small army of cameramen, riggers, ropes professionals, and a safety crew.

Recent findings suggest that “We put together one of the most ambitious camera rigs in TV history,” Smith remarked. “The camera is 1,700 feet high, and we had cameras covering every foot of it.”.

Industry observers note that the crew suffered a minor catastrophe when, on the January 23 shoot date, they awoke to see the building shrouded in fog and buffeted by steady rain. After pushing it back a day, they enjoyed perfect conditions for Honnold’s climb. The cameramen strapped into their harnesses and zipped up ropes on the building’s facade. Honnold and McCandless Honnold stepped out of a white van at street level and embraced, and then Honnold began climbing the building’s metal frame toward the top, and toward a new future.

Industry observers note that “You could tell he was having a lot of fun on a worthwhile endeavor,” Smith claims. “The success of Skyscraper Live at some point comes down to Alex’s authenticity.”.

According to recent reports, the first inkling I got that Skyscraper Live was about to boost Honnold into a new level of fame came a few days before the stunt when I watched a 30-minute interview with him on CNN. Then, in the days after the climb, Honnold was everywhere: Jimmy Kimmel Live, the pages of Hollywood trade magazine Variety, and even on the popular podcast hosted by comedian Hasan Minhaj. The media crush kept rolling, and in fast succession Honnold did lengthy one-on-one interviews with Rich Roll, British celebrity Jay Shetty, entrepreneur Steven Bartlett, and others.

In a recent development, in addition to interview requests, requests for paid public speaking engagements also rolled in, many of which Honnold agreed to. After a few months, Honnold and his team decided to raise his speaking rates. In 2019, Honnold charged a low five-figure fee to speak. For 2026, Significant Speak, a website that allows you to book a motivational speaker, lists Honnold’s fee at above $50,000. Another site, WSB, estimates his fee at $70,000.

According to recent reports, prior to Skyscraper Live, the Latest York Times reported that his fee for the ascent would be $750,000—noticeably low for a professional athlete. But Honnold emphasized that he would have happily climbed the building for free. The comparatively low upfront pay, he claims, has also generated a substantial uptick in revenue afterward.

Sources indicate that “Every segment of earning has grown a bit each year: sponsorship, corporate speaking, and then TV and film stuff,” Honnold says. “Taipei 101 just turned everything up quite a bit.”.

Industry observers note that in many ways, Honnold is charting his own path as a crossover outdoor athlete, who earns paychecks from doing jobs that are only tangentially related to his sport. In a famous scene in Free Solo, Honnold tells a class of schoolchildren in 2016 that his earnings from rock climbing are comparable to what a successful dentist would earn. Now, Honnold notes, that’s no longer the case.

Industry observers note that “I think I’ve exceeded that of any normie jobs,” he says. “Maybe if you owned a dental franchise.”.

Honnold’s long-term financial plan has been to earn enough from climbing to never have to work a normal job in his life. Honnold created that goal long before he had three other mouths to feed and a personal charity to back. The Honnold Foundation supports solar power programs across the globe, and in 2026 the foundation committed $11 million in donations, its largest amount ever.

Now, Honnold states, the lifetime earning goal is within reach.

“I’ll hit that lifetime savings goal in the next year or two,” he notes.

I ask Honnold if the flying, the showing up, and the stress are worth it.

“The pro climbing thing is going to wind down at some point—I’ve always known it,” he claims.

It has been revealed that for three whole hours Honnold is a remarkably good model for the camera lens. He clings to the side of massive boulders, tilting his head this way and that, as a photographer belts out curious orders. The monotone, mechanical personality parodied by Instagram memes is nowhere to be seen. Honnold cracks jokes and tells stories as though he’s addressing a room full of software salesmen in Orlando.

According to recent reports, I ask Honnold if the strategic dad adventures, scheduled between work obligations, are a permanent part of his life as an adventurer. Honnold shakes his head: this phase in his life doesn’t last forever, he reminds me. The babies will get older, the corporate speaking engagements may evaporate, his free time to climb will someday return.

Recent findings suggest that “The things I’m stressed about, I know that they are temporary,” Honnold indicates. “At some point I’ll be able to slow things down a bit.”.

Sources indicate that whether or not that’s true is, of course, up for debate. Those who know him best are dubious that Honnold will ever back away from the breakneck balancing act. In many ways, the demands of family and work, when added to climbing, give Honnold the level of commitment he needs to thrive.

“With Alex it’s gonna be nonstop—not just with climbing but also with work and family,” Weidner indicates. “He has always seemed really uncomfortable with any downtime. To him, it’s just a waste.”.

Wright puts it more bluntly: “Alex would be miserable with an easy life.”.

“Alex wants to be charging headlong at all times at everything he’s doing,” Wright adds. “He’s just taken that ethic for climbing and is now applying it to the crazy opportunities that are open to him. I think it’s impossible for him to say no.”.

Recent findings suggest that thus, there are likely to be more flights, more hurried ascents, and more gray hairs in Honnold’s future—in addition to another media project that showcases his skill and bravery to the widest audience possible. As we drive back to the family cabin, I ask Honnold if he’s done soloing buildings, to which he replies with an emphatic no. The next chapter of Skyscraper Live hinges on finding the right skyscraper. The world’s highest building, the 2,717-foot Burj Khalifa in Dubai, is the obvious choice. But the war with Iran has made that structure abnormally complex.

Industry observers note that “There are five or six others in China that are also a bit of a risk,” he indicates. “Not off the table, but not preferred.”.

According to recent reports, the energy is high at the family cabin when we arrive: neighbors buzzing by to say their goodbyes, a cadre of relatives in town to share the afternoon, and McCandless Honnold preparing afternoon snacks for the kids. Honnold and I leave the chaos for the garage climbing gym to continue our conversation. As we bounce from climbing to money to fame, I can tell that the pull of his life is feeling more like a strong tug. The babies will be home soon. Then, houseguests will arrive. Then, packing for Europe. His phone buzzes with texts and missed calls.

Industry observers note that we wrap up the interview, and Honnold gives me a firm handshake. He’s been more than generous with his time. And now it’s off to the next family outing, corporate speaking event, or climbing crag, to do what he has always done best, which is being Alex Honnold.

In a recent development, topo Athletic's new Traverse 2. (Photo: Topo Athletic).

Sources indicate that it’s a toss-up what thru-hikers think about more: food, or their feet. After all, when you’re on the trail hour after hour, day after day, you can’t replenish calories fast enough. And at that pace, small flaws in shoe design can rapidly magnify into a full-blown sufferfest. But with the right footwear—a shoe that provides the perfect combination of stability, durability, and comfort—thru-hikers can stop worrying about their feet and get on with daydreaming about their next cheeseburger.

Thru-hikers have already discovered Topo Athletic’s Traverse low-top hiking shoe, and appreciate its traction, toughness, and tailored fit on the longest trails. The latest iteration, the Traverse 2, builds on that foundation with fresh details geared specifically to multi-month objectives like the Appalachian Trail and Pacific Crest Trail.

Industry observers note that extended adventures demand durability, so the Traverse 2 features a newly introduced, high-abrasion mesh upper with strategically placed overlays that fend off trail debris without adding extra ounces (which is key when deciding what is and isn’t worth the weight on lengthy thru hikes). Protecting feet from dirt, rocks, and precipitation is also essential for logging long trail miles day after day, so Topo Athletic added its universal gaiter attachment system to the Traverse 2.

It has been revealed that the Traverse 2 is built for anything the terrain throws at you. The full-length Vibram ® Megagrip outsole digs into technical, rocky, and wet trails, while a flexible forefoot rock plate beefs up underfoot protection. The three-piece midsole platform is designed for all-day hiking with a heavy pack, with a softer foam on the base of the heel and a firmer foam on the medial arch for maximum stability. Topo Athletic’s FKT insole features TPU beads not only for rebound and comfort, but also to help the shoes drain and dry in a flash. The shoe’s 5-millimeter drop hits the sweet spot to provide a more natural gait across long distances. And of course, the brand’s signature fit combines a roomy toe box with a snug fit around the midfoot and heel for a naturally comfortable feel.

Recent findings suggest that all this comes in a streamlined package that keeps you light on your feet. The Traverse 2 weighs in at 9.2 ounces for a women’s 7 and 11.2 ounces for a men’s 9. It’s the kind of shoe that lets thru-hikers forget about their feet and focus on the adventure (or visions of that next cheeseburger).

Sources indicate that topo Athletic, based in Framingham, Massachusetts, empowers people to move better for life. Rooted in the belief that every step shapes the journey, Topo builds performance-driven footwear with a focus on lasting comfort and durability, all with its signature fit.

The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy.
  • It has been revealed that the Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world.
  • While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the latest skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

It has been revealed that the Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to major wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more latest climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

Sources indicate that in 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

In a recent development, “Yangshuo means a lot to me,” indicates Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Industry observers note that given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

Take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”.

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

Industry observers note that “We always have a substantial, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he states. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”.

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

Recent findings suggest that “Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”.

Arc’teryx is a Canadian company based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.

#21366. Tech Report: What We Learned When Sabastian Sawe Finally Broke the 2-Hour Marathon

Tech Report: What We Learned When Sabastian Sawe Finally Broke the 2-Hour Marathon

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the early 2010s, the idea of breaking two hours in the marathon went from pipe dream to attainable goal.
  • It has been revealed that like the four-minute mile, first toppled by Roger Bannister in Oxford, England, in 1954, the two-hour marathon is an enticing target.
  • It has been revealed that after that much-watched effort, Kipchoge became the torchbearer for breaking two hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the early 2010s, the idea of breaking two hours in the marathon went from pipe dream to attainable goal. For the first decade of the new millennium, the world’s top distance runners had been chipping away at it. Paul Tergat first breached the 2:05 barrier with his 2:04:55 mark at the 2003 Berlin Marathon. Haile Gebrselassie ran 2:03:59 at the same race in 2008, and by 2014, Dennis Kimmetto held the record with a 2:02:57, less than seven seconds per mile away from sub-two.

It has been revealed that like the four-minute mile, first toppled by Roger Bannister in Oxford, England, in 1954, the two-hour marathon is an enticing target. It’s an even number in a popular event. It’s easy to describe, and therefore easy to market. Perhaps that’s why Nike decided to pour millions of dollars into their Breaking2 project, starting in 2016, bringing Eliud Kipchoge within 30 seconds of the barrier on May 6, 2017, in an exhibition race on the F1 track in Monza, Italy.

It has been revealed that after that much-watched effort, Kipchoge became the torchbearer for breaking two hours. His next attempt in 2019 came with a perfectly flat looped course, a roster of pacers blocking the wind, controlled nutrition on a controlled course, and a finishing time of 1:59:40. Kipchoge demonstrated the world that sub-two was possible. He made history. But he didn’t do it in a race.

It would take a special set of circumstances to see the result in a record-eligible setting. An elite athlete would need the right training, the right weather conditions, the right competition. The previous nine times the world record had been set, these circumstances came together in a fall race (Berlin eight times, Chicago once). But at the 2026 London Marathon on April 26, the stage was set. Sabastian Sawe had returned to defend his title, lining up alongside 2025 Chicago Marathon champion Jacob Kiplimo and Yomif Kejelcha, an accomplished track runner making his marathon debut.

According to recent reports, on a clear, calm day, the three runners followed pacers through the halfway mark in 60:29. To drop below two hours, they would need to run the second half at least a minute faster, cutting the pace by at least five seconds per mile from their average of 4:37. By mile 18, Kiplimo was falling off the back, leaving just Kejelcha stubbornly hanging on to the shoulder of a hard-charging Sawe. Sawe continued ratcheting the pace down, running the eighth 5K of the race (from approximately mile 21 to 24) in a blistering 13:42—4:25 per mile. But Kejelcha hung on, staying on Sawe’s shoulder until the final four minutes.

When he crossed the line in a time of 1:59:30, Sawe became the first runner to break two hours in a record-eligible marathon. Eleven seconds later, Kejelcha became the second. Kiplimo’s third place time of 2:00:28 was also faster than the previous world record. The two-hour barrier wasn’t broken by an exceptional individual in a one-off performance. Ultimately, a true race with fierce competition and constant pressure was what it took to bring Sawe into the history books.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh).

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-latest TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

Industry observers note that the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

Follow This ‘Map of Quietude’ to the Most Silent Trails in Sweden

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taking in one of the many gorgeous views along the quiet Swedish coast (Photo: Andrea Bussell).
  • According to recent reports, the invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden.
  • Outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health concerns: noise pollution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taking in one of the many gorgeous views along the quiet Swedish coast (Photo: Andrea Bussell).

According to recent reports, the invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden. “The only condition? You have to stay quiet.” Surrounded by apple orchards, with the sea just out the door, this idyllic place would be available to a few lucky travelers—as long as we maintained an air of “quietude” during our respective stays.

Outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health concerns: noise pollution. According to the European Commission, prolonged exposure to loud, chronic noise is the second largest cause of health problems contributing to cardiovascular disease, sleep disturbances, and stress-related health concerns. Spending time in naturally quiet environments can help relieve those symptoms.

Skåne is a region renowned for its restorative pastoral and seaside landscapes, unique rural culture, farm-to-table restaurants, and heritage traditions. Within it, The Map of Quietude—a list of 26 places mapped by a professional sound engineer—leads to many spots along Skåne’s 1,000+ miles of hiking trails. Each spot’s silence has been measured to ensure distinctly healing experiences.

According to recent reports, I found that pausing in them to take in the stillness and beauty added something beyond a typical travel or hiking experience. It gave me insight into the true frequency of a place and what it offers: peace, an immersion in rejuvenating slowness, and awe. After my days in silence on the coast, I’ve rounded up some best trails where you can easily experience these locations of quietude, while also taking in interesting communities, historic sites, and some of Scandinavia’s most beautiful wildernesses. Sweden’s nature-centric way of life includes the right of public access, or allemansrätten, which allows hiking or camping almost anywhere in the countryside with the expectation that you will respect the land.

Distance: 7.5 miles Part of the Öresund Way, this loop is worth a detour from inland Skåne to discover a car-free island where people come to bike and hike. You can also get some of the region’s best cardamom buns at Hven Durum, a family-run bakery and mill.

A quick ferry will bring you to this tiny slip of seaside heaven. Walk along the coastline and through a species-rich nature reserve for sweeping views of the Öre Sound and Copenhagen skyline. Ven’s southern headland, södra udde, is a nature reserve and designated place of quietude. See an active, mid-20th-century lighthouse nearby. Or, check out the site of 16th-century Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe’s observatory.

Distance: 7.4 Miles (bonus summit extends to 11.4 miles).

Starting at the edge of the Kulla peninsula in northwest Skåne, you’ll trace roughly seven and a half miles of mostly flat shoreline south from the small fishing village Mölle. One of Sweden’s first seaside resorts at the turn of the 19th century, city dwellers came here for their nature fix. Back then, Mölle was steeped in scandal when, after long hikes, men and women began swimming together in the sea nearby, something that was unthinkable at the time.

Sources indicate that the route explores nature reserves and gnarled pine forests and winds past beaches and historic towns. You’ll even pass remains of Kulla fälad, a vast historic pasture that served as a shared grazing land for livestock for centuries. In some places, ancient drystone walls are still visible. You’ll end in Höganäs, a globally renowned center of stoneware and ceramics production. It’s also a great place to explore a burgeoning creative community. Stop by The Hub Höganäs to experience local life, where artists sell heritage-steeped crafts, and locals gather for events. If you’re looking for a great place to eat, try Hubben, a local spot run by friendly Swedes.

Industry observers note that to visit a place of Quietude, start in the spectacular Kullaberg Nature Reserve. From there, head to Håkull, the region’s highest peak. The summit offers panoramic views of the sea and Danish coastline. It will add about four miles to your trek.

Industry observers note that distance: 117 miles For over 100 miles, the Österlen Way traverses the southeast corner of Skåne. This is Sweden’s famed culinary region. It’s also where my Stay Quiet Cabin was located. Starting in the medieval town of Ystad, the Österlen Way follows the Baltic Sea coast. It passes through nature reserves, national parks, and fishing villages, with inland stretches through ancient forest.

Among other fascinating stops, you’ll pass the hilltop stone circle, Ales Stenar. This is often referred to as “Sweden’s Stonehenge” for its similarly mysterious origins. The trail has two spots of Quietude. The first is Meditationsplatsen, a circular enclosure where people come to meditate. There’s also Gislövshammar Quarry, a 19th-century limestone quarry on the coast of its namesake fishing village. This area is known for its many orchards, farms, and excellent independent shops and bakeries.

In a recent development, distance: 113 miles This breathtaking route hugs the wave-swept coastline of the Öresund Strait. From north to south, it passes through historic fishing villages and dramatic landscapes. It combines previously mentioned trails and quiet spots (Håkull, Mölle to Höganäs, and Ven Island) with two additional places of Quietude. There are the historic open-air cold bathing houses Pålsjöbaden and Hilleshögs dalar valley.

It has been revealed that hikers pass beaches, meadows, dunes and cliffs, and enter pine forests. The trail varies in difficulty before finishing with a loop around the Falsterbonäset Peninsula. Stone Age graves, medieval castle ruins, and views of the Danish coast keep things interesting. The final legs of the trail provide ample opportunities for birdwatching. It enters nature reserves that are internationally renowned habitats for many of Northern Europe’s migratory birds.

Distance: 994 miles At just under 1,000 miles (1,600 km), the region’s Skåneleden trail is a long-distance route that traverses a vast amount of the countryside’s changeable terrain. You’ll encounter rocky coast, verdant forest, national parks, and nature reserves. There are also historic sites like castles and stone circles.

The Skåneleden Trail is divided into seven sub-trails by geographic area. There are 148 sections (encompassing all the previously mentioned routes). Many individual sections make for great day hikes. Or, combine them for longer treks over multiple days or weeks. Several sections are near train or bus stations, making transportation easy. Basic campsites with wind shelters and bathrooms are available along the way for those seeking a longer adventure.

**You can hear 60-minute field recordings of birdsong, waves, and wind from each of the places of quietude mentioned above on Visit Skåne’s website or Spotify.

Industry observers note that I’ve spent the past couple of years turning my backyard into an outdoor oasis. Of all the upgrades I’ve made, the two I use and appreciate most are the Plunge Original Cold Plunge Tub and Plunge Standard Sauna.

I use both regularly, whether it’s after a day skiing or biking, a morning workout, or when I need a break from my computer. I suddenly have a lot more friends, too, but I’m sure that’s unrelated.

Plunge’s Black Friday sale is offering up to 30% off cold plunges and 25% off saunas. They’re still a major investment, but if you’ve been considering either one, now is a good time. Here’s my experience owning both and why I recommend them.

In a recent development, I’ve written before about my firm belief that I’m a better person after jumping into an alpine lake. Unfortunately, living in Salt Lake City, where watershed restrictions put many of our nearest alpine lakes off-limits to swimming, I can’t always get my natural cold-water fix when I need it. But I can walk into my backyard.

Sources indicate that in the summer, I use the cold plunge for recovery and relief. We hosted a yard sale on one of the hottest days of the year this July, and I spent the afternoon sneaking behind the garage for a quick dip every hour. It was glorious.

Mine stays at a relatively civilized 55 degrees Fahrenheit, although the Pro Chiller can bring the water down to 37 degrees. Five to 10 minutes is plenty for me. Whether I’m recovering after a few hours on my mountain bike or simply need to clear my head, being submerged in cold water forces me to stop thinking about everything else for a few minutes and just breathe. I get out feeling more awake and clear-headed.

Industry observers note that there’s some science to back up that feeling, too. As Outside contributor Greg Presto reported in his article on eight common cold-plunging mistakes, studies have found evidence of short-term mood improvements and reduced muscle soreness, though many of the broader health claims remain unproven. Regardless, I feel better after using it, and that’s enough for me.

Industry observers note that the model currently on sale has since been updated, but the original-generation tub I’ve used for roughly 18 months has held up well outdoors. It’s roomy and comfortable, and the app lets me adjust temperature, set session times, track progress, and follow Plunge’s guided challenges.

In a recent development, because the chiller keeps the water consistently cold without requiring bags of ice, the convenience means I actually use it, which is more than I can say for the several yoga mats I’ve purchased over the years. Maintenance has been much easier than I expected, too. The app reminds me when it’s time to treat the water or clean the filter, and both are quick, infrequent tasks that haven’t required much effort on my part.

Sources indicate that in the winter, I love alternating between the cold plunge and sauna. In Outside’s guide to the best home saunas, contributor Dean Stattmann named Plunge’s sauna and cold tub bundle the best option for contrast therapy, citing the convenience of controlling both from your phone. I couldn’t agree more.

In the fall, I schedule the sauna to heat up while I’m at my morning ski fitness classes. I come home, climb in, and, if I’m feeling brave, follow it with a cold plunge. It’s the perfect morning ritual before eight hours in front of my computer. Once ski season is here, I’ll be firing it up when I’m leaving the hill so it’s hot by the time I get home.

In a recent development, I chose Plunge’s traditional cedar sauna because it’s compact enough to fit in my side yard, looks good, and smells incredible. It takes some time to heat up, usually about an hour to reach 180 degrees Fahrenheit when it’s 40 degrees outside.

The standard size is advertised to fit up to five people. While I’ve managed to squeeze myself and three girlfriends inside, it’s most comfortable with two people. The fold-up benches are a smart detail if you want more floor space for movement and stretching rather than seating.

One thing worth knowing before you buy: Installation is a project. The sauna requires a dedicated electrical circuit, so factor in that you may need to hire an electrician. You can assemble both products yourself, but I opted for professional assembly, which you can arrange when you order.

It has been revealed that once it’s up and running, it’s hard to beat having your own personal wellness center a few steps from your back door, especially before or after a day outside. Neither product is a casual purchase, but both are well worth it to me.

Sources indicate that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

In a recent development, with all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

Recent findings suggest that however, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Sources indicate that unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

In a recent development, beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

In a recent development, there are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern Upcoming Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Substantial Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Recent findings suggest that spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the Latest Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

In a recent development, perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

In a recent development, winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

It has been revealed that desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

Industry observers note that on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries rapidly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

Industry observers note that my favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

Below are a few of our favorite climbing deals on climbing shoes, ropes, purpose-built pants, and more gear that our editors and testers love.

While not a top pick in our recent shoe guide, we reviewed the Katana Lace in 2024 and called it an excellent shoe for edging and precision placements. It’s also great in narrow cracks and pockets. This is a good first performance shoe for the climber starting to think more about progression, and a great shoe for a climber who cares about performance, but doesn’t want an insanely uncomfortable pair to push their absolute limits. I’ve been climbing in the Katana since last winter and have found it a joy to wear in hand cracks, finger cracks, steep routes, and technical climbs with edging in the gym and on all types of rock. It’s not so great as a comfortable, all-day pair on moderates, or for slab, in my opinion.

Our favorite rope for trad climbing (as of fall 2026), the Black Diamond 9.4mm dry rope balances durability, sleekness, and light weight. During our testing process, we took massive whippers, found ourselves hangdogging on steel permadraws, didn’t obsess over the dirt that got into our rope, and ran the 9.4 over grainy lips on sport pitches and across arêtes and edges on mixed and traditional pitches, as well. After months of testing, the rope barely showed any wear, which is notable for a 9.4 that feels skinny in hand and climbs as smooth and airy as an ultra-light—great for rope drag on monster sport climbs or zigzagging trad leads.

In a recent development, at the time of publication, only the 70m was in stock, with low inventory. If you’re climbing in low-moisture areas, you could get the same rope without the dry treatment (also 20% off), or save 20% on the 9.6mm version if you don’t mind the larger diameter (this version is a bit pricier because it’s bipatterned, making it easier to find the middle—worth the premium, in our opinion).

Our best all-around harness of fall 2026, the Black Diamond Solution uses what it calls Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. Our testers loved the contoured hip support and the durability of this harness. “I took hundreds of falls and [the Black Diamond Solution Guide] gets the highest praise I can give a harness, which is that I never even thought about my harness after a fall,” one of our testers said.

Our top all-around men’s climbing pant of 2025, Black Diamond’s Alpine Light Pants feature a mobility-friendly design. One of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. Continental Divide Trail Southern Terminus Monument to Be Relocated Due to Border Wall

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A section of steel wall along the U.S.—Mexico border (Photo: PATRICK T.
  • Sources indicate that hikers can once again access the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail, more than two weeks after border wall construction closed down the southernmost 1.1 miles of the trail, the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) says.
  • It has been revealed that the southern mile of the trail had been closed since late October, when crews began widening the road that runs along the border fence and installing a second length of wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A section of steel wall along the U.S.—Mexico border (Photo: PATRICK T. FALLON / Contributor via Getty).

Sources indicate that hikers can once again access the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail, more than two weeks after border wall construction closed down the southernmost 1.1 miles of the trail, the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) says. But with the official end of the route now trapped between two sections of steel barrier, the obelisk that marks the terminus will need to be moved.

It has been revealed that the southern mile of the trail had been closed since late October, when crews began widening the road that runs along the border fence and installing a second length of wall. Since 2025, that stretch has fallen inside the Fort Huachuca New Mexico National Defense Area, created when the Trump administration transferred 110,000 acres administered by the Bureau of Land Management to military control.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday, the CDTC said it had received confirmation that hikers would once again be able to access the terminus. As before the closure, anyone entering the NDA needs to apply online for a permit from Fort Huachuca and undergo a background check; additionally, hikers who aren’t U.S. citizens need to be chaperoned by a permitted hiker who is.

In a recent development, “This closure came at a critical time for southbound hikers,” the CDTC said in a statement. “Completing the 3,100-mile trail is a monumental achievement, and the construction activities at the border created dynamic changes to the permitted NDA access in place during the past year.”.

However, the construction has created a upcoming concern: The Crazy Cook monument—the stone obelisk that marks the official end of the Continental Divide—is now sandwiched between the two steel barriers that make up the under-construction border wall. In an email, Audra Labert, the CDTC’s director of communications, stated that while the organization had received reports that hikers had still been able to reach the monument by passing through the construction area, that arrangement is likely temporary.

“Authorities are now confirming plans to move the obelisk outside of the barrier walls for hikers to access, and passages between the barriers will eventually close,” Labert wrote. While it’s not clear when that could happen, the CDTC warned that the government would likely close the terminus to hikers again while it relocated the monument.

Sources indicate that construction on the border wall has complicated thru-hikers’ ability to access the southern termini of several long trails over the past year. In addition to the CDT, the federal government permanently closed access to the Arizona Trail’s southern terminus last November, a move that Matthew Nelson, the executive director of the Arizona Trail Association told Backpacker was “nothing less than a desecration.” In addition, authorities briefly banned Pacific Crest Trail hikers from touching the border wall this spring before abruptly reversing course. The under-construction barrier continues to figure in access and conservation fights along the southern border, with the Supreme Court recently ruling that the administration could continue construction of a new stretch of wall in Substantial Bend National Park.
