#21357. Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3128 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christina making coffee while camping at Significant Bend (Photo: Abigail Wise).
  • “WE ARE VERY close to being able to see Carroll Crater!” Christina Koch shouts across the campground, glancing up from her moonscope.
  • It has been revealed that the NASA astronaut is bent over a small tube that looks like a telescope, attached to a tripod.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christina making coffee while camping at Significant Bend (Photo: Abigail Wise).

“WE ARE VERY close to being able to see Carroll Crater!” Christina Koch shouts across the campground, glancing up from her moonscope.

It has been revealed that the NASA astronaut is bent over a small tube that looks like a telescope, attached to a tripod. A nearly full moon illuminates her curly hair, with her tent and a field of scraggly creosote bush behind her. The Big Bend National Park campsite is large enough to sleep eight people, but it’s just the two of us here tonight. Even at 10 P.M., the temperature hovers in the mid-70s. It’s already past my bedtime, but Koch and I came to the park to witness what happens in the sky after dark.

According to recent reports, “If you look to the lower left, there’s a dark spot, almost like a mole. Carroll Crater is a little up to the left of that,” Koch says as I bend down to look through the lens, the dark splotches of the moon suddenly massive and detailed to my right eye.

Recent findings suggest that koch and the other three astronauts on the 2026 Artemis II mission named Carroll Crater after colleague and mission commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife. Mission specialist Koch, Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen made history in April 2026 when they completed a ten-day-long mission around the moon, traveling a record-setting 252,757 miles from Earth, livestreaming the event, and going viral along the way. It made Koch the first woman to travel around the moon, adding another record to her list, which also includes the longest spaceflight by a woman (328 days throughout 2019 and 2020), and embarking on the first all-women spacewalk on October 18, 2019.

It has been revealed that FIVE MONTHS AFTER the Artemis II crew touched down in the Pacific Ocean, Koch and I met in Big Bend to go on our own small mission: nighttime photography. Last night, September 26, was a full moon, and it still looks massive, bright, and round above the Chihuahuan Desert tonight. The only way you can tell it’s no longer full, Koch tells me, is that you can spot a little bit of the Terminator in the upper right corner. The Terminator, the line that divides the side of the moon that’s glowing from the one going into shadow, looks like a sliver of darkness that shifts the moon’s craters into 3D.

“Imagine seeing that when it’s literally this significant in your view,” Koch notes, holding her hands wide.

We’ve spent the evening on a couple-mile hike and scramble up to Balanced Rock to photograph the stars and moon. Balanced Rock is a massive boulder suspended between stacks of rocks on either side so that it appears to hover above the ground. Sitting next to the boulders, Koch set up her tripod and snapped shots of the massive, orange moon rising and the stars sparkling above the syenite rock formations. She even managed to capture the shooting star we both spotted streaking above.

It has been revealed that photography is her hobby, she tells me. She’s been taking pictures since she did so for her college paper at North Carolina State University, from which she holds multiple degrees in physics and electrical engineering.

According to recent reports, her love of photography came in handy for her space missions. NASA, which features an entire photography training team, worked with Koch and the rest of the Artemis II crew ahead of their historic trip to optimize documenting photos of the moon and Earth from space. They had to learn how to use a wide lens as the Artemis II crew occupied a very small vehicle, how to use the proper f-stop and shutter speeds, and how to take more technical photography, too, to report back on anything that appeared broken and other details for the on-the-ground engineers.

Photography wasn’t the only arts-based training the Artemis II crew took on prior to their mission. The four astronauts decided to seek out and collaborate with a poet to assist them in better describing what they saw in space. Koch still trains with the poet today. “He helps me a lot with metaphors and language, but also just seeing the beauty in things,” she states.

The crew’s holistic approach is, in many ways, different from how older generations of astronauts prepared for space travel. The Apollo Generation, which included astronauts like Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, who became the first people to walk on the moon in 1969, focused on thousands of hours of moonwalk and lunar surface simulations and reduced gravity training. While practical, technical skills were vital to the Artemis II astronauts, too, they also concentrated heavily on team dynamics: the crew embarked on a National Outdoor Leadership School (NOLS) trip together, a common practice today for NASA teams. “We made so many commitments to being a crew that loved and trusted each other,” states Koch. “NOLS was one of the things that we did when we learned a lot of those actual skills to keep us in a good place and keep us friends.”.

Industry observers note that another focal point for the Artemis II crew was learning about the meaning behind their destination. “We worked with cultural experts on the moon and tried to cultivate a deeper understanding of the many facets of where we were going, not just the scientific ones,” claims Koch.

It has been revealed that but for the differences in training approaches and communication styles throughout history, the narrative around space exploration has, in many ways, remained the same. “Beautiful concepts like love and peace, and going for all of humanity, those have always been a part of it,” says Koch. “There is almost no one who went [to space] and didn’t have beautiful things to say.”.

Recent findings suggest that AFTER A COUPLE of hours taking pictures near Balanced Rock, Koch and I are back at camp, eating dinner under the moonlight. She’s cooked up some simple couscous on a backpacking stove and finishes it with a handful of pine nuts.

“This is how low-key I am,” indicates Koch, gesturing to her pot. “It’s practically plain couscous, and I’m so excited for it because I was such a dirtbag backpacker for so long. This is very standard and kind of nostalgic.”.

Recent findings suggest that over the years, Koch, who’s 47 years old, has developed an arsenal of dirtbag and outdoors skills. She’s an accomplished climber—mostly sport, trad, and ice—and skis both downhill and cross-country. Despite growing up near the ocean in North Carolina, where her dad taught Koch and her four siblings how to sail, she didn’t begin surfing until her mid-thirties; now it’s one of her favorite sports. She also loves trail running, but after struggling with hip dysplasia for years (the trip to Big Bend was a few months after she had a hip replacement), Koch took up triathlons instead to balance out the running with cycling and swimming. In order to do so, she had to learn to swim distances, which she tackled in her mid-forties. “It took me like two years to learn to swim. I’m very uncoordinated,” Koch insists.

Sources indicate that one of Koch’s biggest adventures, outside of the Artemis II mission, took place in 2006 when she and some friends climbed Mount Kenya. The group ascended the 17,058-foot mountain, which requires technical climbing to reach the highest summits, without a porter. The first night camping on the trip, Koch opened the door of her tent after hearing a strange noise; a sea of glowing eyes reflected back at her as a herd of wild buffalo passed by. “I was like, ‘We’re going to get trampled and die,’” she notes.

According to recent reports, luckily, the herd moved on without incident, but Koch had another problem: she quickly realized that she hadn’t packed enough food for the ascent. That same night, a ranger came by and had cut his finger very badly but didn’t have a way to sew up his wound. Koch and her friends had a first-aid kit on hand and helped patch up his injury in exchange for a can of beans.

According to recent reports, the beans, along with the food she did pack, helped fuel her through the week-long backpacking trip, in which she and her friends carried a lot of weight, hauling their climbing gear up to the technical section of the mountain. While they didn’t make it all the way to the summit they were targeting, they did climb for a stretch of it. “We made it higher than you could walk up,” claims Koch.

Coming off the mountain, though, the climbers were out of food and cash, and rather than hike another eight miles, they managed to scrounge together their very last coins to ride a bus back to town. “I must have lost so much weight,” she claims. “My pants were hanging off of me, and we were very hungry.”.

But they arrived at their target hotel safely and used their credit cards to book a room. “I will never forget the next morning we were eating at an all-you-can-eat breakfast buffet,” indicates Koch. “It was the funniest dichotomy of going from really feeling like we were at the end of our line, coasting out on fumes, to being completely OK and in the borderline lap of luxury. It was just so ridiculous.”.

Sources indicate that professionally, Koch spent several years of her early career traveling to remote, isolated landscapes, conducting scientific research. She always wanted to be an astronaut, but wasn’t interested in pursuing the typical paths astronauts often follow, such as obtaining a degree in aerospace engineering or getting a pilot’s license. “I want to be in nature, not flying over it, so that was just never a hobby that really called my name,” she notes.

It has been revealed that so while Koch has dreamed of being an astronaut since she was a child, she wasn’t going to give up her interests to pursue some kind of checklist to become one. Instead, she followed her passions for science and nature into often harsh environments. She worked as a research associate for Raytheon Polar Services, stationed in Antarctica, where the area closes down for months at a time due to extreme cold and darkness. “There’s no mail, no fresh food, no people in or out for eight months,” Koch claims. “That was something I went and did when I was 25.”.

She also worked as an electronics and instrument technician in Greenland, Alaska, and again in Antarctica before traveling to American Samoa in 2012 as a station chief for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). It was there, while stationed in American Samoa, that she met her husband, Bob Koch, who at the time was working as a GIS coordinator.

Recent findings suggest that during a time before smartphones and internet access were a given, Bob quickly figured out that Koch drove by a favorite surf break of his 45 minutes east of where he lived on her way to work each morning. So Bob asked Koch to take a photo of the surf on her commute, and then send it to him over the reliable internet at her laboratory. “She was my surf report buddy, and then obviously things took off from there,“ claims Bob, who now works for the Army Corps of Engineers. “We called it Peter Pan Island.”.

Not long after meeting, Koch decided to apply to become an astronaut, and when she was accepted in 2013, she and Bob moved to Houston, Texas, where NASA’s Johnson Space Center is based and where the couple now lives with their dog, Sadie. “Going from a full-on dirtbag lifestyle to the most regimented, military-like astronaut training, with these requirements and proficiencies, was like whiplash for me,” states Koch, who used to view more conventional career paths as selling out or growing up. “Everything I did was towards free time and the outdoors and very minimal requirements in life.”.

In a recent development, but her thinking soon shifted as she embraced her newly introduced job. “I used to think that all of these people working really hard don’t know what life is really about,” she says. “And then I realized, actually, maybe it’s totally OK to work really hard for something and make a difference.”.

WHEN ARTEMIS II launched into space from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, the four crewmembers had prepared themselves, each other, and their loved ones for the risks and reality of the adventure they were undertaking. In preparation, the Kochs bought a Sprinter van.

It has been revealed that “[Bob] was trying to figure out what do you do when your wife goes to the moon?” indicates Koch. “You can’t go to work; you’re not going to be able to concentrate. If you’re sitting at home, you’re going to be worried. So he organized a road trip with his friends.”.

Bob devised a initiative: Mission Break 80, in which he and his friends would golf and surf their way from Florida, where Artemis II introduced, to San Diego, where the crew was set to land. They’d camp along the way in his newly introduced van, which proudly displayed an Artemis II magnet. As a joke, Bob created Mission Break 80 patches to match. And while he only made it as far as Houston in the van, the distraction largely worked.

Sources indicate that “Going surfing every morning took me away from my phone for two hours, or the act of setting up camp and being outside just created a calming effect,” claims Bob. “That was my way of coping with the mission: actually spending time outdoors, away from devices, but just close enough in case I needed to get a call.”.

Industry observers note that bob got two half-hour calls with Koch during the mission, one on day three and the next on day seven. He took the first call from the beach with wet hair and waves in the background.

In a recent development, one thing the crew and their families had not prepared for was how many people would watch the Artemis II mission worldwide. “Moon joy,” the excitement of the 2026 orbit, as it was dubbed, went viral. NASA reported more than 149.4 million views of the launch, splashdown, and lunar flyby on its own platforms alone. An estimated 400,000 people gathered in person to watch the launch in Florida, according to Smithsonian Magazine. “They kind of caught lightning in a bottle,” claims Bob. “I think it was a combination of the synergy of the crew collectively and all their unique personalities and kind of how they played off each other. And I think it was just some timing where people really wanted a positive story that they could follow and all rally around.”.

While #moonjoy was trending on every social platform, Koch and the rest of the Artemis II crew were oblivious to the buzz on the ground. “We never dreamed it would become what it was,” claims Koch. “We actually might never know what happened on Earth while we were gone,” she continues. “Earth had a party for us, and we weren’t there.”.

On the second of their two allotted calls, Bob realized he had to let Koch know how popular the mission had become. He told his wife that she and her colleagues were inspiring people down on Earth. “I told her how proud I was and how inspirational she and the crew and mission were,” he indicates. “I remember she teared up.”.

Koch remembers the call vividly, too. “He was like, ‘Tina, I need to tell you something. Something is happening down here. You guys are having an impact. You’re moving the needle,’” she recalls.

“It’s funny because when you cry in space, your tears well up in your eyes, and they just stay there,” claims Koch, explaining that the lack of gravity makes it so that tears don’t fall. “I was wiping my buoyant tears, and I was like, ‘That’s all we ever wanted…’ When we designed our mission patch, it was ‘A II;’ we made it look like the word ‘all.’ That was our goal: for all.”.

IT’S NEARLY NOON and the sun is blazing in Balmorhea, Texas. Koch and I just met up to cool off in the world’s largest spring-fed swimming pool, a 1.3-acre body of brisk water in the high desert of West Texas. We’re taking a dip with the locals—kids splashing and shrieking with delight, groups of women floating on inner tubes, and a handful of scuba divers—before driving out into the 91-degree desert to hike and camp.

As we chat and tread water, I glance down to see schools of fish darting around our legs. “Sometimes they bite,” Koch told me earlier, “which is kind of fun!”.

If I look long enough, with a little luck, I might even see a turtle, one frequent swimmer mentioned when I arrived. Koch claims she spotted them last time she was here on a van trip.

“I’m going to go do some laps and look for turtles,” she tells me, snapping on her goggles and doing the breaststroke over toward the deep end, which reaches 25 feet.

According to recent reports, I follow her, trailing behind, gazing into the sparkling, royal blue water. Behind me, a group of teens is taking turns launching off a diving board, and a small family is gearing up to scuba dive. We’ll need to head out soon if we want to snag a camping permit before the park’s visitor center closes. Koch knows it’s time to get going, too.

Sources indicate that “I’m just going to jump off of the high dive one time before we go,” she announces, making her way to the opposite side of the pool. As I watch, she climbs out and walks briskly to the edge. She hesitates briefly as she eyes the water below. Then, she jumps, suspended in space for just a moment before she splashes back down to Earth.

Sources indicate that abigail Wise is the brand director at Outside. She’s been fascinated with space since her mom sent her to a science space camp one summer in elementary school. These days, she’s been known to drag her own kids out to watch meteor showers in the middle of December near their home in northern Fresh Mexico—and insists it’s worth every whine.

#21356. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2708 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Sources indicate that directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Recent findings suggest that behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Sources indicate that directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Recent findings suggest that behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

In a recent development, posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

According to recent reports, when Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

Sources indicate that when he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

In a recent development, “The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

According to recent reports, “Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he notes, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

Sources indicate that in a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees indicates. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

Sources indicate that “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza states, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

In a recent development, while the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

According to recent reports, as the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Sources indicate that without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

Recent findings suggest that while sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Industry observers note that glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Sources indicate that over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

According to recent reports, of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

Recent findings suggest that while Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Recent findings suggest that since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he notes. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

It has been revealed that since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque claims that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I mentioned, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

In a recent development, inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”.

Industry observers note that while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque notes.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque claims the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he states. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an crucial mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

According to recent reports, for all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he indicates.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily remarked yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

In a recent development, looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he states.

Don’t let the obligation of holiday shopping take up too much of your time—the editors at Climbing have determined what we believe are the best gifts for the climber in your life, whether a gym, sport, trad, or ice climber, a burgeoning mountaineer, an all-arounder, or someone who hasn’t tried climbing yet, but is eager to get started.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh new set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

It has been revealed that ocun’s newly introduced Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

According to recent reports, last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

Recent findings suggest that edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one.

Recent findings suggest that the Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a new, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

In a recent development, the Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional big-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

Apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

Black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

Climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

Industry observers note that what gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? By donating to Access Fund you become a member of the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, who tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens new ones.

The daughter of Climbing’s editor in chief, Maya Silver, has worn the Black Diamond Momentum kids’ climbing shoe for the past four years. Once she finally outgrew it this last summer, the decision was easy to order her another pair. Like the adult Momentum shoe, the Momentum kids is super comfortable thanks to its neutral last, easy to get on/off with a simple Velcro closure, and offers sufficient performance for most little crushers.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents.

A chipmunk chews its way into a hiker's backpack. (Photo: Stanislav Sablin/Getty Images).

One of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents. I love watching squirrels chase each other around tree trunks, and I may or may not have had a “pet” chipmunk in one of my cabins during a horseback guiding season. I talk to marmots when I’m alone, and hearing the chirp of a pika makes my day. But I draw the line at the little buggers crawling over my face in a shelter, chewing through my trekking pole straps, or getting into my food bag.

This is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite. While no one I know has a perfect mouse-proofing strategy, here are a few tips and tricks to help keep rodents at bay and protect your pack pockets, straps, and food.

The most vulnerable parts of your gear are the deliciously salty pack straps, trekking pole straps, and pockets where you’ve forgotten you left food. While keeping your straps clean is easier noted than done after days of sweaty hiking, reducing the tantalizing salty odors will work wonders in keeping sodium-fiending rodents away. If you can, dunk your straps in running water a few times throughout the day, and especially at night when you get to camp.

You can also drip a few drops of hand sanitizer onto trekking pole straps to make them less appealing, and tucking a dryer sheet into salty pockets or around hammock straps can also work as a rodent deterrent. Finally, always stash your trekking poles upright in the ground to keep the straps less accessible.

It has been revealed that the bear hang is a time-honored backcountry art form, but if you’ve ever seen an acrobatic mouse shimmy down the rope and land a perfect 10 on your backpack, you know this protective measure doesn’t translate perfectly to rodent-proofing. The solution, as many of us have seen in high-traffic trail shelters, is something I call the Mouse Swing. This is simply your standard piece of paracord or bear-hang rope, but with a barrier tied in the middle.

According to recent reports, I’ve used everything from a (clean!!) tuna can to a quart-size yogurt container lid. Punch a hole in the can or plastic lid, run your string through the hole with knots to secure it in place, and you’ll have a lightweight, highly functional barrier between your pack and the string. Make sure your bag is a few feet above the ground or shelter floor to prevent high jumpers from making the leap.

Along with salty straps, mice, rats, and squirrels are highly attracted to food smells. The worst pocket destruction I encountered was when I carefully hung my pack from the rafters of a shelter but forgot to remove the remains of an energy bar from the pocket, and an industrious mouse chewed right through the material. Don’t forget to check your pockets for lip balm, energy gels, or the remains of your lunchtime protein bar.

While a hard-sided bear canister is the best protection against animals getting into your food supply, I prefer not to carry the bulky, heavy contraption unless it’s required in the area. The next best thing is the Ursack Allmitey, a heavy-duty food bag made from Spectra, a specialized material with one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios out there. Once tied properly closed, it’s next to impossible for critters to chew through or squeeze through the opening. If you’re in an area where rodents are the only concern, you can size down in bulk to the Ursack Minor, a Kevlar bag that isn’t tough enough to stand up to bears, but can keep smaller toothy critters at bay.

In a recent development, I’ve also used RatSacks for food drops in the desert. They’re heavier than the Ursack Minor, but have proven virtually indestructible against desert rodents, and some national parks like Canyonlands lend them out for free. These are made from stainless steel mesh with a heavy-duty Velcro closure at the top, and while they aren’t bearproof, I’ve never had a smaller animal bust through the dense metal mesh.

Finally, if scent control is your primary priority, you can further streamline your gear with LokSak OPSAK bags. These won’t prevent sharp little teeth from chewing through them, but the polyethylene material and secure zip tops are completely odorproof and can keep curious squirrels and chipmunks from testing them in the first place.

I hesitate to write this since it’s such a Massive If, but if you’re camping somewhere that the risk of running into a bear is zero, you can bring smelly items into your tent. This isn’t foolproof—you run a risk of an unusually bold mouse chewing into your tent—but by and large, most small rodents will be deterred by your massive sleeping form and won’t bother trying to break in.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (763 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On May 29, a Nepali high-altitude worker named Hillary Dawa Sherpa ran out of oxygen while descending Mount Everest at the edge of the Death Zone.
  • Hillary Dawa’s improbable story of survival ignited a debate about safety and ethics on the world’s highest peak.
  • He was originally hired to work as a seasonal cook at the Camp II setup of low-cost Nepali guiding company Himalayan Traverse Adventures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On May 29, a Nepali high-altitude worker named Hillary Dawa Sherpa ran out of oxygen while descending Mount Everest at the edge of the Death Zone. Days went by, and officials assumed he was dead. And then, six days after vanishing, he crawled on his hands and knees out of the Khumbu Icefall toward Base Camp, where he was rescued by camp workers.

Hillary Dawa’s improbable story of survival ignited a debate about safety and ethics on the world’s highest peak. And the 57-year-old wasn’t supposed to have been on Everest’s highest slopes in the first place.

He was originally hired to work as a seasonal cook at the Camp II setup of low-cost Nepali guiding company Himalayan Traverse Adventures. The company had just two paying clients for the 2026 season: Chris Thrall, a British ex-Royal Marine, and Mariusz Chmielewski, a plumber from Poland.

But late in the expedition, Hillary Dawa was asked to guide Thrall up the mountain, after Himalayan Traverse Adventures sent one of its experienced climbing Sherpas home.

“I was only supposed to be a cook, but they offered me 10,000 Rupees a day to climb with the clients,” Hillary Dawa told Outside. “I didn’t even want to go to Everest this year.”.

Recent findings suggest that outside reached out to Himalayan Traverse Adventures but did not receive answers for this story. Hillary Dawa stated tech giant management believed Thrall was incapable of making it above Camp IV. But Thrall eventually reached the summit. Hillary Dawa and Chmielewski turned back before the top and retreated to Camp IV. On the descent, the company’s other climbing Sherpa sped ahead down the peak, while Thrall, Chmielewski, and Hillary Dawa continued together. They were racing toward the May 29 closing date, which is when Sherpas would remove ladder bridges from the Khumbu Icefall.

Sources indicate that “I was carrying eight empty oxygen tanks and the client’s sleeping bag,” Hillary Dawa remarked. “If I lost an oxygen bottle, they would deduct $250 from my salary, so I had to bring it all down.”.

Eventually, he ran out of oxygen and sat down to rest, telling Thrall to continue. Thrall and Chmielewski reached Camp II at 23,000 feet and radioed for help, saying Hillary Dawa was in trouble. But Himalayan Traverse did not mount an immediate search and rescue mission.

Days went by with no sign of him. A larger firm, 8K Expeditions, eventually debuted a rescue. Assuming nobody could survive that long without food and water, reporters increased the season’s fatality rate to six. His family prepared funeral rites at a monastery in Kathmandu.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, high on the mountain, Hillary Dawa fought to live. After regaining consciousness, he inched down, stopping at abandoned tents to search for scraps of food and water. At the Khumbu Icefall, he found safety ropes buried under snow and ladder bridges intact. He was within sight of Base Camp when another disaster struck—a ladder bridge collapsed, sending him plunging 50 feet into a crevasse. He caught a safety rope, which saved his life.

In a recent development, “I looked down and saw a small ledge of snow,” he said. “I kept my head straight and slid down the rope and landed on the ledge. And that’s when my leg broke.”.

According to recent reports, injured but alive, Hillary Dawa spent the next two and a half days on the precipice. He survived by eating a few pieces of candy and a packet of instant coffee, rationing the calories carefully and sucking on ice to moisten his mouth. On the night of June 3, his fifth day alone on Everest, an avalanche rumbled into the crevasse. Hillary Dawa braced for the worst.

“I thought about God,” he noted. “I prayed: ‘Either let me die here or help me get out.’”.

He lived. And in the morning, he saw that the slide had created a snow ramp to the surface. Using his good leg, Hillary Dawa pushed himself backward to the surface. Severely dehydrated and weak, he spent the next day and night crawling through the labyrinth of ice, eventually emerging near Base Camp. Within a few hours, Hillary Dawa became a global sensation.

While his ability to survive against seemingly impossible odds is the stuff of legend, his ordeal also raises uncomfortable questions about who bears the greatest risks on Everest, and what happens when expeditions cut corners.

Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside.
  • Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

It has been revealed that audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing new climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

“She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

“With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” said Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

It has been revealed that pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

Pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

Two Hikers Rescued from Wet Snow and Freezing Temperatures Deep in the White Mountains

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A view west from Mount Bond in New Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness.
  • Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in Newly introduced Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.
  • It has been revealed that hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A view west from Mount Bond in New Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness. (Photo: MikeCherim / Getty Images).

Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in Newly introduced Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.

It has been revealed that hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes. The first involves taking the Lincoln Woods Trail, which is generally a 19.9 mile round-trip hike with 3,959 feet of elevation gain and right now partially closed. The second route takes hikers up the Zealand Trail, covering 19 miles and up to 4,947 feet of elevation gain.

While it isn’t clear which route the duo took to Mount Bond, 23-year-old Ethan Fena and 21-year-old Matthew Nakota were more than 10 miles into their hike near the summit when they encountered winter trail conditions.

Industry observers note that although they’d packed lights, food, and water, Latest Hampshire Fish and Game (NHFG) said the pair had hiked the route without overnight and winter equipment, leaving them struggling to warm themselves. By the time the duo called for help, they’d assembled a makeshift shelter in an attempt to warm up and allow their gear to dry.

Industry observers note that NHFG said that conservation officers initiated a rescue operation, using ATVs to transport volunteers with the Pemi Valley Search and Rescue Team to the area. Rescuers reached the pair at about 11:45 p.m., and helped them begin the descent back to the trailhead. The whole party arrived safely at the parking lot at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 15th.

In the wake of the incident, Fresh Hampshire Fish and Game officials reminded hikers to consider factors like shortened daylight hours and failing temperatures before heading into the mountains.

In a recent development, this incident comes just 11 days after two 18-year-olds became stranded on Mount Washington after getting caught on the peak without headlamps. The two hikers reached the Lakes of the Clouds AMC Hut and discovered that it had been closed for the season when they realized they needed help. The group used an emergency shelter located at the hut until rescuers reached the hikers and helped them descend the mountain.

It has been revealed that some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your newly introduced boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

It has been revealed that originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

Having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

Industry observers note that it’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk revealed how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

It has been revealed that luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

After breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

Recent findings suggest that the new Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Sources indicate that the Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

Sources indicate that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

Sources indicate that the pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the new film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

Have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

Sources indicate that the oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

Note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

According to recent reports, I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a newly introduced collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the space of three years, Amflow has made a name for itself by designing versatile e-bikes that excel on mountain trails, gravel roads, and other routes that begin where the pavement ends. Now, it’s introducing a latest pair of city-oriented e-bikes that exemplify the brand’s expertise in engineering, support, and safety. The UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro might be Amflow’s first purpose-built commuter models, but they’re the culmination of everything the brand built since its inception.

Most riders spend their time in urban environments, so it makes sense that Amflow set out to design a bike that shines across the broad spectrum of daily use. The UE Carbon series builds on the brand’s history and is more than a mere concession to urban riders. This bike feels natural from the very first pedal, regardless of a rider’s size, riding style, or itinerary, and it’s tailor-made for commuting, running errands, heading on a fitness ride, and everything in between.

The foundation of the UE Carbon’s everyday adaptability is its rider-friendly design. The bike’s sleek carbon frame keeps its weight down; at 46 pounds, it’s nimble enough for navigating dense urban cores, as well as light enough for lifting onto public transport and into a storage space. A step-through design promotes an upright riding posture, which—combined with substantial adjustability and easy-to-maneuver 26-inch wheels—allows people of varying sizes to get in the saddle. The geometry also supports loads up to 44 pounds in the front and 59 pounds at the rear with the right accessories. The rear rack’s MIK HD compatibility adds quick-release modularity, letting the bike adapt to urban commuting, family outings, and light outdoor adventures.

From a technical perspective, the UE Carbon reaps the benefits of Amflow’s excellent array of components. Both the standard and Pro models feature the premium Avinox M2 motor, which provides 1,100W of peak power and 125 Nm of torque. The robust drive system cruises 30% inclines with ease, with a smooth overall feel and low noise output (approximately 45 dBA). Plus, with a maximum range of 82 miles via a 600Wh removable battery, the UE Carbon can go for multiple days without a recharge.

Recent findings suggest that as with all Amflow bikes, there’s top-notch tech throughout. Both the UE Carbon and Carbon Pro include electronic shifting (the major difference between the two models is the drivetrain and its components: a 10-speed electronic rear derailleur and chain on the Carbon, while the Pro has a three-speed electronic internal geared hub and Gates drive belt). The 1.4-inch cockpit display grants intuitive control of the bike’s functions with a simple, clean interface, and riders can connect to an Apple Watch and the Avinox Ride app, which also includes a lost mode. Additionally, an integration with the Apple Find My lets customers track the bike’s location in real time and activate its sound alert. An included frame and battery lock will hopefully ensure you never have to use the lost mode or tracking features.

In a recent development, that suite of features, plus the UE Carbon’s all-around functionality and ergonomic design, makes it the perfect choice for those who want a bike that can handle anything the city serves up. It’s a proud next step in Amflow’s expanded e-bike offerings and is bound to put the brand on even more riders’ radars.

According to recent reports, proudly born in 2023, Amflow is the creation of tech experts with a limitless passion for riding electric bikes. The firm strives to amaze with an unmatched combination of power, range, and performance, hidden in sleek bike bodies. Amflow’s commitment to the e-bike industry is to make its bikes the go-to for all e-bike riders looking to turn any terrain into a wonderland of possibilities.

#21339. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young.
  • As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions.
  • The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert claims, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”.

It has been revealed that kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most crucial role model,” mentioned mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”.

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

It has been revealed that give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

Industry observers note that when your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”.

Recent findings suggest that learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

It has been revealed that some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between substantial and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Recent findings suggest that talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

In a recent development, as parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • It has been revealed that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

It has been revealed that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Recent findings suggest that now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: New Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Industry observers note that print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

💡 Key Takeaways
